title: Lecture 9 — Two-sample MR and polygenic risk scores
text:
Lecture 6 introduced Mendelian randomization (MR) as if one study measured everything: the genotypes, the exposure and the outcome in the same people. In practice that is rare. The large GWAS of LDL cholesterol and the large GWAS of coronary artery disease were done in different cohorts, and both publish only summary statistics (β, SE, P per SNP). Two-sample MR combines those two sets of summary statistics: the SNP → exposure effects from one GWAS and the SNP → outcome effects from another. No individual-level data is needed, which is why it has become the standard way MR is done.
The price is careful bookkeeping. The same SNP must be found in both files, its alleles must refer to the same strand and the same effect allele (harmonisation), and the two GWAS must describe comparable populations. The three MR assumptions do not go away.
The second half turns from causation to prediction. The same GWAS results can be used to add up a person’s many small genetic effects into a polygenic risk score (PRS). MR asks does X cause Y?; a PRS asks who is at higher risk? The lecture’s arc is association → causal inference → prediction.
This page covers what makes MR “two-sample”, the data it needs, the workflow (select instruments, find them in the outcome GWAS, harmonise, estimate, sensitivity analyses, interpret), the practical pitfalls, and then PRS: the formula, the data it needs, how SNPs are chosen, and how a PRS is interpreted and evaluated. It ends with a real study from Gothenburg, given as extra material (Section 9.14), that uses multivariable MR and polygenic scores to ask whether remnant particles are more harmful than LDL particles.

9.1 What makes MR “two-sample”?










One-sample MR
Two-sample MR




Where G → X comes from
The same individuals
An exposure GWAS (e.g. GLGC for LDL-C)


Where G → Y comes from
The same individuals
A separate outcome GWAS (e.g. a CAD consortium)


Data needed
Individual-level genotypes, exposure and outcome
Summary statistics only


Typical sample size
Limited to one cohort

Common confusion: “two samples” does not relax the assumptions. The slides are explicit: two-sample MR does not remove the three assumptions. The instrument must still

be associated with the exposure (G → X, relevance),
be independent of exposure–outcome confounders (independence),
affect the outcome only through the exposure (G → X → Y, exclusion restriction).

The GWAS primer states the same three assumptions and notes that MR “can be employed to assess causal relations between different phenotypes using GWAS summary statistics”, typically when a randomized trial is not feasible (GWAS primer).
What changes is only where the numbers come from. Two-sample MR adds new practical problems on top (Section 9.8): matching SNPs across files, harmonising alleles, and making sure the two GWAS describe comparable people.

  It needs two instruments for every exposure
  It tests the exposure in two separate ancestries
  G→X and G→Y are estimated in different samples
  It removes the need for the exclusion restriction
  The SNP–exposure effects come from one GWAS and the SNP–outcome effects from another. All three MR assumptions still apply.

section: 9.3 Step 1: selecting instruments and the F-statistic
text:
9.3 Step 1: selecting instruments and the F-statistic
The workflow (the slides stress that “the difficulty is in step 1–3”):
1. Select instruments for the exposure (X)
2. Obtain their associations with the outcome (Y)
3. Harmonise alleles
4. Estimate the causal effect
5. Sensitivity analyses
6. Interpretation
Step 1. Identify variants that

are associated with the exposure: genome-wide significant, \(P < 5 \times 10^{-8}\) in the exposure GWAS;
are sufficiently strong instruments: \(F > 10\) (below);
are approximately independent of each other: LD clumping. Pick the SNP with the smallest P (or the highest F), remove the SNPs in LD with it, repeat.

The F-statistic for one SNP is the squared z-statistic of its exposure association:
\[F = \left(\frac{\hat\beta_{GX}}{SE(\hat\beta_{GX})}\right)^2\]
The rule of thumb is F > 10. Below that the SNP is a weak instrument: it explains so little of the exposure that its Wald ratio is unstable and biased (Section 9.8).

F for the slide table. rs1: \((0.08/0.01)^2 = 64\). rs2: \((0.05/0.01)^2 = 25\). rs3: \((0.10/0.02)^2 = 25\). All three pass F > 10.
A SNP at exactly genome-wide significance, \(P = 5\times10^{-8}\), has \(|z| \approx 5.45\) and therefore \(F \approx 29.7\). Any genome-wide significant SNP automatically has F > 10, so F matters mostly when instruments are chosen at a looser threshold.

  F = 6.25; weak, because F is below 10
  F = 0.36; weak, because it is below 1

section: 9.4 Step 2: finding the same variants in the outcome GWAS
text:
9.4 Step 2: finding the same variants in the outcome GWAS
For every selected exposure SNP, look up in the outcome GWAS: effect allele, other allele, effect estimate for the outcome, its SE, and the effect allele frequency if available.
Things that go wrong here, all raised on the slides:

The lead SNP is missing from the outcome GWAS (highlighted on the slide as a seminar discussion point). The usual solution is a proxy SNP in strong LD (\(r^2\) close to 1) that is present in both (6.1), or dropping the instrument.
Are the two GWAS comparable? Same ancestry? Similar sex and age distribution? An effect estimated in one population may not transfer to another.
Are the two samples comparable? Two-sample MR assumes both GWAS sample the same underlying population, just different people.
Genome build (tutorial): if you match on position rather than rsID, both files must use the same build (e.g. both hg19). Positions differ between builds.

“Each G lowers the outcome by 0.03” is the same statement as “each A raises it by 0.03”. Rule: if the effect and other alleles are swapped, flip the sign of the outcome β (and use 1 − EAF). SE and P are unchanged.
Without harmonisation: \(-0.03/0.08 = -0.375\) (X looks protective). With it: \(+0.03/0.08 = +0.375\). Same data, opposite conclusion.

Harmonising against the wrong pair silently flips about half of the SNPs, which drags the IVW slope toward zero or even reverses it. A result that contradicts well-established biology (e.g. LDL-C appearing to protect against CAD) is a strong signal to recheck this step first.

section: 9.6 Step 4: the Wald ratio and IVW
text:
9.6 Step 4: the Wald ratio and IVW
One SNP: the Wald ratio.
\[\hat\beta_{MR} = \frac{\beta_{GY}}{\beta_{GX}}\]
Slide example: \(\beta_{GX} = 0.08\), \(\beta_{GY} = 0.03\) → \(\hat\beta_{MR} = 0.03/0.08 = 0.375\). It answers: how much does Y change per unit change in genetically predicted X?
Several SNPs: inverse-variance weighted (IVW) MR.

Plot each SNP as a point: x = SNP effect on the exposure, y = SNP effect on the outcome.
The slope of a line through the origin is the causal effect.
IVW is a weighted mean of the per-SNP Wald ratios. The weights are typically

\[w_j = \frac{\beta_{X_j}^2}{SE(\beta_{Y_j})^2}\]
A SNP gets a large weight if it moves the exposure a lot (strong instrument) and its outcome effect is precisely estimated. The same number comes out of a weighted regression of \(\beta_Y\) on \(\beta_X\) through the origin with weights \(1/SE(\beta_Y)^2\) (derivation in 6.7).

section: 9.7 Interpreting an MR estimate: units, and “genetically predicted ≠ intervention”
text:
9.7 Interpreting an MR estimate: units, and “genetically predicted ≠ intervention”
The unit of the exposure decides what the number means. The slides use systolic blood pressure (SBP) as the exposure and pulse wave velocity (PWV, m/s) as the outcome:








Exposure unit
Estimate
Reading




per 1 mmHg SBP
1.05
per 1 mmHg higher SBP, PWV is 5% higher


per 1 SD SBP (e.g. 120 → 126 mmHg)
1.2
per 1 SD higher SBP, PWV is 20% higher



Both describe the same biology on different exposure scales. Always state the unit.






WarningCheck the arithmetic: 1 mmHg vs 10 mmHg



The slide continues “per 10 mmHg, PWV increase 50%”. That is the additive approximation (10 × 5%). If 1.05 is a ratio per mmHg, effects multiply: \(1.05^{10} = 1.63\), i.e. +63% per 10 mmHg. The two agree only for small changes. The same logic applies to odds ratios: an OR of 1.2 per SD becomes \(1.2^2 = 1.44\) for 2 SD, not 1.4.








ImportantGenetically predicted exposure ≠ intervention effect



Highlighted in red on the slides. Genotype acts from conception, so an MR estimate reflects a lifelong difference in the exposure, and lifetime exposure builds risk. A drug started at age 60 changes the exposure for a much shorter time. MR estimates are therefore often larger than what an intervention in adulthood achieves, and the direction is the more reliable part.

9.8 Pleiotropy, sensitivity analyses and practical pitfalls
Horizontal pleiotropy does not disappear in two-sample MR. Add sensitivity estimates next to the main IVW result:







Method

(Details on weighted median and MR-Egger: 6.8.)
Practical problems specific to two-sample MR (slides):









Problem

More on winner’s curse (GWAS primer): it is common for highly polygenic traits, where many variants with small effects sit just above the significance threshold; effects “close to the discovery threshold tend to be overestimated”. The gold standard correction is to re-estimate the effects in an independent replication cohort with no shared or related individuals. In MR this is why instruments are ideally selected in one sample and their β_GX taken from another.
Why weak instruments behave differently with and without overlap. A weak SNP’s β_GX is mostly noise. In two independent samples the noise in β_GX is unrelated to β_GY, so the ratio is diluted toward zero. When the same people are in both GWAS, the same confounding that links X and Y in those people leaks into both betas, pulling the estimate toward the ordinary (confounded) observational association.

  Toward zero, as with any weak instrument
  Toward the confounded observational estimate
  Away from zero in the opposite direction
  Not biased, since overlap only affects SEs
  With complete overlap, weak-instrument bias pulls toward the confounded observational association. With no overlap it pulls toward the null.


  Makes β_GX too small and inflates the MR estimate
  Changes the sign of β_GX for about half of the SNPs
  Makes β_GX too large and shrinks the MR estimate
  Only affects the outcome GWAS, not the exposure
  SNPs that pass the threshold tend to be the ones whose β happened to come out high. A too-large denominator gives a too-small Wald ratio, biasing toward the null.

title: Lecture 9 — Two-sample MR and polygenic risk scores
section: 9.9 PRS vs MR: same GWAS, different question
text:
9.9 PRS vs MR: same GWAS, different question









Mendelian randomization
Polygenic risk score




Question
Does variation in X causally affect Y?
Can genetic information predict who is at higher risk?


Level
Population: one causal estimate
Individual: one score per person


Uses
A few strong, valid instruments
Many SNPs, including weak ones


Pleiotropy
A threat (exclusion restriction)
Fine: any predictive signal helps



Association → causal inference → prediction. A GWAS finds variants associated with a trait. MR uses them to test causation. A PRS asks: even if each effect is small and each variant is common, what if we add many variants together? “PRS takes us back to the individual again.”
Definition (course book, quoting the tutorial): a PRS is a “single value estimate of an individual’s genetic liability to a phenotype, calculated as a sum of their genome-wide genotypes, weighted by corresponding genotype effect size estimates derived from GWAS data”. The terms genetic risk score (GRS), polygenic score (PGS) and PRS are used interchangeably. The book gives a GRS two goals: to predict the likelihood of developing a disease, and to estimate how much predictive capacity the associated variants capture.
Why many variants? Most complex traits are polygenic (the LDL exercise found > 100 SNPs acting through many genes), and most SNPs have a tiny effect by themselves. Most people carry some risk alleles. Only the sum separates people meaningfully.

9.10 The PRS formula
A PRS is calculated for an individual \(i\) as the sum over \(M\) SNPs of allele dosage × estimated effect:
\[PRS_i = \sum_{j=1}^{M} G_{ij}\,\hat\beta_j\]

title: Lecture 9 — Two-sample MR and polygenic risk scores
text:
9.11 Two datasets: discovery and target
A PRS analysis (preferably) needs two data sets:









Discovery sample (tutorial: base data)
Target / validation sample




Provides
The β estimates (GWAS summary statistics)
Individual genotypes, the phenotype/outcome, covariates


Typical size
Very large (a consortium GWAS)
Smaller cohort where the score is computed and tested



The course book describes the same split as base data (GWAS summary statistics) and target data (“an independent sample from the base data used for PRS analysis”), and stresses that the effect allele and genotyping method must be known and equal in both (course book).
The two must be independent (tutorial; also course book and GWAS primer: “accuracy measurements can be inflated if the discovery GWAS and the target cohort share individuals”). If people from the target sample were also in the discovery GWAS, their own outcomes helped estimate the β’s, and the PRS–outcome association in the target sample is inflated. This is the PRS version of the sample-overlap problem in 9.8. Close relatives across the two samples cause a milder version of the same inflation.
Other checks from the tutorial’s QC list: confirm which allele is the effect allele in the base GWAS (otherwise the score points the wrong way), remove ambiguous (palindromic) and duplicated SNPs, use the same genome build, and prefer target samples of ≥ 100 individuals.

title: Lecture 9 — Two-sample MR and polygenic risk scores
section: 9.12 Choosing SNPs: clumping + thresholding, and shrinkage
text:
9.12 Choosing SNPs: clumping + thresholding, and shrinkage
Two problems with using raw GWAS output directly:

Many estimates are imprecise. Most SNP β’s are mostly noise, and the top hits are inflated by winner’s curse.
Linkage disequilibrium. Strongly correlated SNPs carry the same signal. Summing them counts one locus many times, which is “not good in prediction models”.

The classical approach: clumping + thresholding (C+T).

Clumping: keep the lead SNP from each locus (as in Step 1 of MR).
Thresholding: include SNPs with a GWAS p-value below a threshold, and typically try several thresholds (e.g. \(5\times10^{-8}\), \(10^{-5}\), \(10^{-3}\), 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1) and keep the one that predicts best (tutorial).

Common confusion: weak instruments are a problem in MR but welcome in a PRS. Now we may include weak instruments, “remember the weak learners from stat learning!” Each SNP adds a little signal; no single SNP needs to be valid on its own, only the sum needs to predict. Pleiotropy does not matter either.
The statistical learning route (slides):

Instead of forcing independence by clumping, estimate the correlation between SNPs and put it into the model (LD-aware methods).
Use LASSO (penalized regression) with a train/test split: SNPs with large effects that are partly sampling noise are shrunk toward zero. This directly counteracts winner’s curse.

The GWAS primer calls C+T “pruning and thresholding”, “the simplest and most practical method”; more complex methods model the LD structure or add functional information to estimate the effects better (GWAS primer). The course book lists penalized regression (LASSO or ridge) and Bayesian approaches, which also handle LD, and warns that they must be tuned to avoid overfitting (course book).
C+T includes a SNP at its full β or excludes it (β set to 0). Shrinkage methods keep more SNPs but pull every β toward zero by an amount depending on how noisy it is (tutorial).






WarningOverfitting the threshold



If you try 10 thresholds in the target data and report the best one, that “best” R² or AUC is optimistic. Choose the threshold in one part of the data and report performance in another (a validation set or cross-validation) (tutorial).

title: Lecture 9 — Two-sample MR and polygenic risk scores
text:
9.13 Interpreting and evaluating a PRS
What a PRS means (slides):

A PRS has no natural unit. It is a relative measure, usually close to normally distributed and often standardized (mean 0, SD 1), so results read “per SD of PRS” or “top 5% vs the rest”.
It does not directly translate into a probability of disease. A high score says “higher risk than others”, not “a 30% risk”.
Most often a PRS predicts less than age, sex, SBP etc.

How to evaluate it (slides):







Question
Measure




Does it add to discrimination?
AUC: the probability that a random case has a higher predicted risk than a random control (0.5 = coin toss, 1 = perfect)


Is it calibrated?
Do predicted risks match observed risks (e.g. predicted 10% → about 10% get the disease)?


Does it add to prediction?
Compare age + sex + smoking + SBP with age + sex + smoking + SBP + PRS: the gain in AUC (or R², the incremental R² in the tutorial) is what the PRS adds



The model comparison written out (GWAS primer):
\[H_0:\ \text{Phenotype} \sim \text{covariates} + e \qquad H_1:\ \text{Phenotype} \sim \text{PRS} + \text{covariates} + e\]
with covariates such as age, sex and ancestry (principal components). The variance explained by the PRS term alone is the difference between the two models: \(R^2\) for a continuous trait, a pseudo-\(R^2\) from logistic regression for a binary one.
What the course material adds about accuracy:







Point
Source




AUC > 0.75 is considered informative for screening; > 0.99 is needed as a diagnostic aid. Calibration curves check for overfitting
course book


The maximum possible accuracy is capped by the SNP-based heritability of the trait
GWAS primer


One of the best PRSs (glaucoma): top decile has 4.2-fold higher risk than the bottom 90%
GWAS primer


A high odds ratio per SD does not mean good screening: at a 5% false-positive rate, a published CAD PRS would miss 85% of people who develop the disease. Reclassification measures (e.g. the net reclassification index) are more clinically relevant than OR or AUC
GWAS primer


Accuracy decays with ancestral distance from the discovery GWAS (mostly European), because allele frequencies and LD differ
GWAS primer, course book


Clinical utility is “yet to be established”; ethical, legal and social issues, e.g. genetic determinism and stigma
course book, GWAS primer



Why the added value is usually small. The PRS is partly correlated with the traditional risk factors (e.g. a PRS for CAD partly works through LDL and SBP), so part of its signal is already in the base model.





Simulated data (not from the slides). Left: the PRS distributions of cases and controls overlap heavily, so the score cannot sort individuals well on its own. Right: yet disease prevalence rises steeply across PRS deciles, so the score does separate groups.




Reading the figure (tutorial, Fig. 5): in real data (BMI PRS in UK Biobank, explaining ~5% of BMI variance) the prevalence of severe obesity rises steeply in the top strata, but most obese individuals still have an average or low PRS. A high-risk group can be identified; an individual cannot be predicted with confidence.

  The PRS is not associated with CAD at all
  It adds little discrimination beyond the base model
  The base model is badly calibrated and useless
  The PRS is a better predictor than age and sex
  An association can be clearly significant while the gain in AUC is small. Part of the PRS signal is already carried by the traditional risk factors.


  A has a 2% absolute risk of developing the disease
  A will develop the disease, since +2 SD is extreme
  A’s genetic liability is high relative to others
  A’s risk is exactly twice the population average
  A PRS is relative. +2 SD places A in roughly the top 2.5% of scores; turning that into an absolute risk needs a calibrated model with the baseline risk.

section: 9.14 Extra material: remnant cholesterol, LDL and CHD in UK Biobank
text:
9.14 Extra material: remnant cholesterol, LDL and CHD in UK Biobank






NoteExtra material, not required reading



This study was provided as extra material, separate from the course’s reading material. It is included because it applies the lecture’s methods to real data. The section has no exam flag.


(extra material) Björnson E, Adiels M, Taskinen M-R, Burgess S, Rawshani A, Borén J, Packard CJ (2023). “Triglyceride-rich lipoprotein remnants, low-density lipoproteins, and risk of coronary heart disease: a UK Biobank study.” European Heart Journal 44:4186–4195. A Gothenburg study that uses almost every tool from Lectures 4–9 and continues the course’s LDL story.
The question. Triglyceride-rich lipoproteins (TRL) and their partly digested remnants also carry cholesterol and one apoB per particle, like LDL. Is a remnant particle more atherogenic per particle than an LDL particle, or is CHD risk simply a function of the number of apoB particles?
Design, mapped to the course:




Step in the paper
Course concept




GWAS in UK Biobank (~350,000 people not on lipid-lowering therapy), adjusted for age, sex and genetic PCs 1–5
GWAS covariates, population stratification (4.4)


SNPs with P < 5×10⁻⁸, MAF > 0.01, LD-pruned at r² < 0.1 (20 Mb window)
Instrument selection, clumping (9.3)


SNPs associated with lipoprotein(a) removed (28 SNPs) → 1125 SNPs
Guarding against a known horizontal pleiotropic pathway


Multivariable MR with IVW: several exposures (apoB, LDL-C, TRL/remnant-C) in one model, each effect adjusted for the others
Extension of IVW (9.6)

ImportantThis is the only lecture with instructor EXAM tags



The course’s reading guide says: “The slides with information that we will be testing on the exam are marked with a small text ‘EXAM.’” Every section below with the 🎯 Instructor-flagged EXAM badge carried that marker. Treat these as the highest-confidence exam content in the course. The instructor also posted “Lecture 7 - questions.pdf” with example exam questions. All 11 are on the Exam practice page with model answers.
Up to now, each analysis tested one thing: one SNP, one exposure. Omics data flips that around. You measure hundreds or thousands of molecules (here 955 microRNAs) in a few dozen samples and ask which of them differ between groups. Three problems follow in a chain: high dimensionality → noisy measurements → multiple testing.
The measurements are noisy because the lab process adds its own variation, so the data must be cleaned (background correction, normalization) before any biology is compared. With few samples per feature, the ordinary t-test becomes unreliable, and the fix is to let the features borrow strength from each other (the moderated t-statistic in limma). And with 955 tests at once, about 48 will look “significant” by chance, so the significance cutoff has to change: Bonferroni controls the chance of any false positive, Benjamini–Hochberg controls the proportion of false positives among the hits.
The lecture is built around a real study: miRNA profiling of small intestinal neuroendocrine tumours (siNETs), which found tumour subtypes and a survival biomarker, miR-375.
This page follows that study from sample to result. The BH and Bonferroni calculations have worked tables, an R exercise and a drill that generates new problems. Be able to do them by hand.

7.1 Why high-dimensional data is a different problem
Classical epidemiology asks one question: is exposure X associated with outcome Y? Omics-scale molecular epidemiology asks: which of hundreds or thousands of molecular features are associated with phenotype Y, all in the same analysis.
High dimensionality  ──▶  Noisy measurements  ──▶  Multiple testing

title: Lecture 7 — High-Dimensional Molecular Data
text:
7.2 The siNET case study
Clinical background. Small intestinal neuroendocrine tumours (siNETs) are often diagnosed only after metastasis. Five-year survival is poor but highly variable and hard to predict. Biologically they are distinctive: an unusually low mutational burden and no classic recurrent driver mutations. Tumour initiation is thought to be driven by large-scale chromosomal alterations and epigenetic factors instead. (A useful contrast with AML in Lecture 3: not every cancer is a point-mutation story.)
miRNA recap (Lecture 3): short (~22 nt) non-coding RNAs acting as epigenetic/post-transcriptional regulators: they suppress translation and reduce mRNA stability. Perfect pairing is not needed, so each miRNA regulates hundreds of mRNAs. Altered miRNA expression is found in virtually all tumour types. Aberrant miRNAs act as oncomiRs (promoting cancer) or tumour suppressors, by targeting genes for proliferation, cell cycle, apoptosis, invasion and drug resistance.
Study aim: characterize the miRNA profile of siNETs, looking for clinically relevant molecular subgroups and biomarkers of tumour development and outcome.
Samples: 42 tumours from 37 patients operated for siNET, plus 6 samples of normal small intestinal mucosa.

title: Lecture 7 — High-Dimensional Molecular Data
text:
7.3 The microarray experiment

RNA isolation: with a commercial kit (e.g. miRNeasy, Qiagen) from fresh-frozen tumour tissue (at least 70% tumour cells) and normal mucosa.
Labelling and hybridization: RNA is labelled with a fluorescent dye and allowed to base-pair with known probe sequences fixed on an array (Agilent).
Scanning: a scanner reads fluorescence intensity at every spot. Intensity is a relative measure of how much of that miRNA is present; software turns the image into numbers.
Design details: 955 probes (866 human + 89 viral miRNAs), 4–8 replicate spots per probe (to assess consistency), 48 samples (42 tumours + 6 normal).

7.4 Observed variation = biology + technical noise
\[\text{Observed signal} = \text{biological signal} + \text{technical variation (noise)}\]
Sources of technical variation in this study: RNA extraction, labelling, hybridization, scanner/detection noise and batch effects (developed further for proteomics in Lecture 8, Section 8.6; the principle applies to every high-throughput platform).
Implication: before trusting any biological comparison, remove as much technical noise as possible. That is what preprocessing does.

  To remove the biological signal so only noise is left
  The measured signal also contains technical variation
  To turn relative intensities into absolute concentrations
  Because the t-test cannot be used on log-scale values
  Observed variation = biology + technical noise (extraction, labelling, hybridization, scanner, batch). Preprocessing removes technical variation so remaining differences reflect biology.

section: 7.7 Why the ordinary t-test fails, and the moderated t
text:
7.7 Why the ordinary t-test fails, and the moderated t
The ordinary two-sample t-statistic
\[t = \frac{\bar x_1 - \bar x_2}{s\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{n_1} + \tfrac{1}{n_2}}}\]
where \(s^2\) is estimated separately for every gene/miRNA from only \(n_1 + n_2 - 2\) degrees of freedom: just 4 df for 3 vs 3 samples, a very typical omics size.
Three compounding problems

\(s^2\) is very noisy: with 4 df a feature’s variance estimate is often far from its true variance.
By chance some features get a tiny \(s^2\). Since \(s^2\) is in the denominator, \(t\) becomes huge even when the mean difference is small → false positives.
The ranking is partly driven by noise in each \(s^2\), so real effects with a larger \(s^2\) are missed → lost power.

The solution: the moderated t-statistic, R package limma. Instead of trusting each feature’s own noisy variance, limma uses empirical Bayes to share information across all features: each variance is shrunk toward a common variance estimated from the whole dataset. The result is a moderated t-statistic and p-value per feature.
The shrunken (moderated) variance is a weighted average of the common prior variance \(s_0^2\) (with prior df \(d_0\)) and the feature’s own variance \(s_g^2\) (with \(d_g\) residual df):
\[\tilde s_g^2 = \frac{d_0\, s_0^2 + d_g\, s_g^2}{d_0 + d_g}, \qquad \tilde t_g = \frac{\bar x_1 - \bar x_2}{\tilde s_g\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{n_1} + \tfrac{1}{n_2}}}\]
How shrinkage behaves (a “consequences” slide, also marked EXAM):








Replicates

Each variance is pulled strongly toward \(s_0^2\). This prevents false positives from randomly tiny variances

The moderated variance converges to the ordinary sample variance: you trust the feature’s own estimate








Simulation: 2,000 features with NO true difference, 3 vs 3 samples. Left: the ordinary variance estimates scatter wildly around the true variance (dashed); moderated estimates are pulled toward the common value. Right: features with a randomly tiny s² get extreme ordinary t-values; the moderated t removes most of them.

title: Lecture 7 — High-Dimensional Molecular Data
section: 7.8 Summary: the small-sample problem, in full
text:
7.8 Summary: the small-sample problem, in full
Marked EXAM across three consecutive slides. Close to a model answer for “explain why moderated statistics are needed in omics data”.






NoteModel answer structure



1. The challenge of small sample sizes. Transcriptomics, proteomics and metabolomics routinely measure tens of thousands of features on few biological replicates.
2. The failure of standard t-tests. Each feature’s variance is estimated separately from very few replicates, so the estimates are highly unstable. By chance some are abnormally low → inflated t → false positives; others abnormally high → real effects masked → lost power. Because this instability sits under every p-value, it also undermines the multiple-testing correction afterwards, which assumes well-calibrated p-values.
3. The standard solution. Sharing information across the whole dataset, known as variance shrinkage or empirical Bayes moderation, stabilizes the variance estimates: each is pulled toward a common value estimated from all features. This reduces false positives, recovers power and gives more reliable results after multiple-testing correction (e.g. FDR).

section: 7.9b Tumour vs normal results, and the paired-sample note
text:
7.9b Tumour vs normal results, and the paired-sample note
Result: miR-7-5p and miR-375 were the two most significantly upregulated miRNAs in tumours vs normal mucosa. Several other differentially expressed miRNAs previously reported in the siNET literature also appeared (marked with an asterisk in the paper’s figure).
“Note… Why?” Five patients had paired samples (a primary tumour and a liver metastasis). In the tumour vs normal comparison they contributed only their primary tumour.
Why? Two samples from the same patient are not independent (same patient, same genetic background). Including both would give that patient double weight and bias variance estimates and significance tests. This is a general principle: repeated or paired samples from one subject violate the independence assumption of standard tests.

section: 7.10 The multiple testing problem, with this study’s numbers
text:
7.10 The multiple testing problem, with this study’s numbers
955 miRNAs were tested. If none truly differed, you would still expect
\[955 \times 0.05 \approx \mathbf{48}\]
“significant” hits at an uncorrected \(p < 0.05\).
The logic in three steps:

Every test has its own 5% false-positive chance from noise alone, even for a miRNA with zero effect.
Run hundreds or thousands of tests and those small chances accumulate: some false hits become nearly guaranteed.
A flat \(p < 0.05\) applied test by test turns “5% error per test” into a high chance of at least one error somewhere in the study. For 955 independent null tests, \(P(\geq 1 \text{ false positive}) = 1 - 0.95^{955} \approx 1\).

Conclusion (stated directly in the slides): because this is multiple testing, the significance cutoff itself must change.

7.11 FWER vs FDR
Expect to define, distinguish and calculate both.










FWER (Family-Wise Error Rate)
FDR (False Discovery Rate)




Definition
\(P(\text{at least one false positive among all tests})\)
\(E\left[\dfrac{\text{false positives}}{\text{all positives called}}\right]\), the expected proportion of hits that are false


Philosophy
Even one false lead among hundreds of tests is a failure of the whole experiment: a very strict bar
Accepts a known, controlled fraction of wrong hits and controls how large that fraction is expected to be


Classic method
Bonferroni
Benjamini–Hochberg (BH)




Both start from the same p-values but ask different questions, giving different, non-interchangeable cutoffs.

  The chance of any false positive among the 200 is at most 5%
  About 10 of the 200 hits are expected to be false positives
  Each of the 200 miRNAs has a 5% chance of being a true effect
  Exactly 5% of all 955 tested miRNAs are false positives
  FDR = expected proportion of false positives among the hits: 5% of 200 ≈ 10. “Any false positive at most 5%” is FWER control (Bonferroni).

title: Lecture 7 — High-Dimensional Molecular Data
text:
7.12 Bonferroni: controlling the FWER
Rule: reject \(H_0\) for test \(i\) if
\[p_i \le \frac{\alpha}{m} \qquad \text{equivalently} \qquad p_{\text{adj}} = \min(1,\; p \times m) \le \alpha\]
where \(m\) is the number of tests.
Three properties

Valid for any \(m\), any test type, regardless of dependence between tests: no assumptions about correlation, “always safe”.
Controls the strictest bar, the FWER: a single false positive among all tests counts as failure.
Worked consequence for this study: \(m \approx 955\) → \(\alpha/m \approx 0.05/955 \approx \mathbf{0.00005}\). Many true effects do not survive this, so power collapses when \(m\) is large, which is typical for omics.

title: Lecture 7 — High-Dimensional Molecular Data
text:
7.13 Benjamini–Hochberg: controlling the FDR
The BH algorithm, three steps (reproduce exactly):

Sort the \(m\) p-values: \(p_{(1)} \le p_{(2)} \le \dots \le p_{(m)}\).
Find the largest rank \(k\) with \(p_{(k)} \le \dfrac{k}{m}\,Q\), where \(Q\) is the accepted FDR (commonly 0.05).
Call every test with \(p \le p_{(k)}\) significant. The expected FDR of this set is \(\le Q\).

Key difference from Bonferroni: Bonferroni has one fixed threshold \(\alpha/m\). BH’s threshold \(\frac{k}{m}Q\) rises with rank, so larger p-values can still be significant if they clear the higher bar for their rank. That is why BH finds more true positives.

title: Lecture 7 — High-Dimensional Molecular Data
text:
7.14 Why FDR fits omics data
Four reasons, a strong essay-question candidate (“why is FDR preferred over Bonferroni in omics?”):

Too many tests for Bonferroni. Thousands of tests push α/m toward zero, so most true effects never reach it.
Exploratory, not confirmatory. The goal is a shortlist of candidates, not one make-or-break claim. A small, controlled fraction of false leads is an acceptable price for finding more true positives.
Findings are validated afterwards with an independent method and/or cohort. The siNET study did exactly this: miR-375 was confirmed with qRT-PCR and in situ hybridization in a separate cohort.
Features are correlated. Co-regulated miRNAs (genes, proteins) mean the effective number of independent tests is smaller than \(m\). Bonferroni ignores this and stays needlessly strict; BH copes better in practice.


  Thousands of tests make Bonferroni’s threshold too strict
  Screens are exploratory, and hits are validated afterwards
  Correlated features make the effective number of tests smaller
  FDR guarantees that no false positives are among the hits
  FDR accepts a controlled proportion of false positives; it never guarantees zero. Even FWER control only bounds the probability of any false positive.

section: 7.16b Circular reasoning: testing clusters with the data that built them
text:
7.16b Circular reasoning: testing clusters with the data that built them
The M1/M2 clusters were created from miRNA expression (unsupervised clustering), and then miRNA expression was tested again for differences between those same clusters. The same data is used twice: once to define the groups, again to test them.
This is circular reasoning and inflates significance. Any clustering produces groups that differ in the variables used to build it, almost by construction, so “finding” that they differ is not independent evidence.






ImportantGeneral principle



Do not use one dataset to both discover a grouping and test for differences across that grouping without independent validation (a new cohort) or a correction for the selection.







Pure noise: 500 ‘miRNAs’ in 30 samples with no real groups. Cluster the samples into two groups, then t-test every miRNA between those clusters. Under the null the p-values should be flat (dashed line); instead they pile up near zero.





  The Cox regression was not adjusted for age and gender
  Hierarchical clustering cannot use Euclidean distance
  M1 and M2 were defined from the same miRNA data
  Benjamini–Hochberg is too liberal for 955 miRNAs
  The clusters were built from the expression data, so they differ in that data almost by construction. Testing the same data between those clusters is circular and inflates significance.

title: Lecture 5 — GWAS and Computer Exercise 1
text:
This session was mostly a hands-on PLINK exercise, framed by a short lecture. The lecture turns the GWAS idea from Lecture 4 into a concrete workflow: what the data files look like, how they flow through the software, and what you get out at the end.
Its main new content is about what to do after you have a peak in the Manhattan plot. A peak contains many correlated SNPs. Which one is causal? The lecture lists the tools for narrowing it down (conditional analysis, functional annotation, pQTLs, experiments) and introduces LD clumping, the standard way to reduce each peak to one independent SNP.
The key intuition: statistical independence (low LD) is not the same as biological causality. Clumping gives you independent signals, which is exactly what Mendelian randomization needs in Lecture 6, but the clumped SNP may still only be a proxy for the true causal variant.
This page covers the data structures, the end-to-end pipeline, lead vs causal SNPs, approaches to finding the causal variant, the r² table, LD clumping, computing LD from summary statistics and the practical pitfalls when combining datasets.

5.3 Why neighbouring SNPs show up together
Two distinct reasons many related SNPs appear in GWAS output (the exam could phrase it either way):

Causal biology: one causal SNP really changes gene expression or protein function, which changes the phenotype.
Statistical, not biological: SNPs are inherited together (LD). SNP 1, SNP 2, the causal SNP, SNP 3 and SNP 4 can all look associated only because they are correlated with the causal SNP, not because each affects the phenotype.








Term
Definition




Lead SNP
The SNP with the smallest p-value in a region. Not necessarily causal.


Locus
The genomic region with the associated signal: the cluster of correlated SNPs around and including the lead SNP



The causal SNP may not even be on the array. Arrays genotype a pre-chosen set of known SNPs; if the causal variant is not one of them, it can only be inferred indirectly (LD with genotyped SNPs, or imputation, Lecture 6).

Bands: \(r^2 > 0.8\) very strong LD / close proxy; \(r^2 > 0.5\) moderate to strong; \(r^2 < 0.1\) weak; \(r^2 \approx 0\) essentially independent. A common practical threshold for calling SNPs independent is \(r^2 < 0.01\).






WarningPhysical proximity ≠ correlation



LD is usually strongest locally, but not every nearby SNP is highly correlated:

LD patterns differ between populations (different recombination histories and genetic drift);
\(r^2\) depends on both SNPs’ allele frequencies and the haplotype structure;
two SNPs can be physically close yet have low \(r^2\). You have to calculate it.



LD clumping is the automated procedure that reduces each locus’s correlated SNPs to one representative, approximately independent lead variant. Standard practice, and specifically used before Mendelian randomization (Lecture 6), because MR needs independent instruments. Caveat: the clumped SNP may still only be a statistical proxy for the causal variant.

  SNP 1, because it has weak LD with the lead SNP
  SNP 2, because r² = 0.85 makes it a close proxy
  SNP 3, because it is independent of the lead SNP
  SNP 4, because moderate LD avoids double counting
  A proxy should carry nearly the same signal, so you want the highest r² with the lead SNP. SNP 2 (r² = 0.85 > 0.8) is a very strong LD proxy. Proxy SNPs return in Lecture 6.

section: 5.5 LD when you only have summary statistics
text:
5.5 LD when you only have summary statistics
With individual-level genotypes you can compute both the GWAS association and the LD between SNPs from the same data. With only summary statistics (the usual situation with published GWAS, since they contain no individual data) you need an external reference dataset, such as 1000 Genomes, to compute LD.
Why not one big file with everything? Individual-level genotype data is sensitive, restricted and tied to specific projects, so it cannot be bundled with public summary data. You use a separate, appropriately permissioned reference panel.






ImportantMatch the ancestry



The reference panel’s ancestry must match the GWAS population, because LD patterns differ between populations.

text:
5.6 Practical pitfalls when combining datasets
A “what could go wrong” checklist:







Check
Question




Genomic coverage
Are the same SNPs present in both the GWAS and the reference panel?


Allele compatibility
Is “A1” the same physical allele in both, or is the strand/labeling flipped?


Genome build
Is everything on the same build: hg19/GRCh37 vs hg38/GRCh38?


Identifiers
Working with rsIDs avoids many mismatches: they are stable across datasets



Strands and palindromic SNPs (from the computer exercises). DNA has two strands, and studies do not always report alleles on the same one: A/G in one file can appear as T/C (the complement) in another. For most SNPs this is easy to detect. For palindromic SNPs (A/T and C/G) the complement is the same pair, so a strand flip cannot be seen from the letters. They are resolved with allele frequencies when the frequency is clearly different from 0.5, and otherwise excluded. When the alleles are the same but swapped, the sign of β is flipped. Practise in the computer exercise concepts page.
Two reminders: statistical independence (low LD) ≠ biological causality, and the lead SNP is not necessarily causal; one locus may represent several candidate variants or genes.
The purpose of all this (genome-wide significant, LD-clumped, independent SNPs) is to obtain valid genetic instruments for Mendelian randomization (Lecture 6).

  The reference panel was too large for your sample size
  The effect allele (A1) is flipped between the datasets
  The SNPs were sorted by rsID instead of by position
  The p-values were not corrected for multiple testing
  If A1 in one dataset is A2 in the other, every β for those SNPs flips sign. Always align alleles (and strands) and check the genome build before combining data.

title: Lecture 3 — Recap, Mutations and Genetics
text:
This lecture moves from how one gene works to how variation in genes is described, measured and inherited. It starts with small RNAs that switch genes down (miRNA and siRNA) and the two drug types that hit PCSK9 from different sides. Then it teaches the formal notation used to write a mutation down precisely, the difference between inherited and acquired mutations, and the technologies used to read DNA.
The second half is classical genetics with a statistical eye: Mendel’s laws, what happens when two genes sit close together on a chromosome (linkage), and the population-level version of that, linkage disequilibrium (LD). LD is the single concept that makes GWAS results tricky to interpret in Lectures 4–6, so it is worth understanding here.
The lecture ends with Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium (HWE): simple probability that tells you what genotype frequencies to expect from an allele frequency. You will use the same \(p^2\), \(2pq\), \(q^2\) logic again in Lecture 4.

3.2b Two drugs, one pathway: Leqvio vs Repatha/Praluent
Leqvio (inclisiran): an siRNA drug that lowers LDL cholesterol.

It targets PCSK9 mRNA in liver cells and causes it to be degraded.
Less PCSK9 protein is made.
PCSK9 normally promotes LDLR degradation, so more LDL receptors stay on liver cells.
More LDLR means more LDL-C cleared from the blood.

Delivery: the siRNA is chemically linked to a sugar called GalNAc, which binds ASGPR receptors, highly expressed on liver cells (hepatocytes). The GalNAc–siRNA complex is taken up into the liver cell, the siRNA is released and loaded into a protein complex that finds and degrades PCSK9 mRNA. GalNAc works as an “address label” that sends the drug to the liver rather than the whole body.
Repatha (evolocumab) and Praluent (alirocumab): monoclonal antibodies, proteins engineered to bind one specific target. They bind free circulating PCSK9 protein in the blood and stop it from binding LDL receptors on liver cells. More LDLR stays available.

title: Lecture 3 — Recap, Mutations and Genetics
text:
3.6 Mendelian genetics: vocabulary and laws
Genetics is the study of how genes and traits pass from parents to offspring. Gregor Mendel found the basic principles by breeding pea plants and studying single-gene traits (seed shape, flower color, plant height).
Core vocabulary (exactly what short-answer questions target):







Term
Definition




Locus (pl. loci)
A specific physical position on a chromosome


Homologous chromosomes
The two copies of essentially the same chromosome, one from each parent


Allele
An alternative version (DNA sequence) found at a particular locus


Genotype
An individual’s genetic makeup: which alleles they carry


Phenotype
The observable trait that results (in part) from the genotype


Dominant allele (B)
Affects the phenotype when at least one copy is present


Recessive allele (b)
Affects the phenotype only with two copies


Homozygous
Two identical alleles: BB (homozygous dominant), bb (homozygous recessive)


Heterozygous
Two different alleles: Bb



Mendel’s three laws

Law of Dominance: in a heterozygote the dominant allele determines the phenotype and the recessive allele is masked (Bb → dominant phenotype).
Law of Segregation: an organism carries two alleles per gene, but they separate during gamete formation so each gamete gets only one (Bb → B gametes or b gametes, never both).
Law of Independent Assortment: alleles of different genes are inherited independently of each other, except when the genes lie close together on the same chromosome (linkage, next section).


  The person shows the recessive phenotype because b is present
  Each gamete from this person carries either B or b, not both
  The person’s gametes all carry both B and b in equal amounts
  Alleles of B and of other genes are always inherited together
  Segregation: the two alleles separate into different gametes, so each gamete carries one. The phenotype (dominant) is the Law of Dominance; inheritance across genes is Independent Assortment.

title: Lecture 3 — Recap, Mutations and Genetics
text:
3.7 Linkage, recombination and linkage disequilibrium
Recombination (crossover) happens during meiosis: homologous chromosomes exchange segments. This is what lets alleles of genes on the same chromosome be reshuffled.
Genetic linkage. Genes physically close on the same chromosome are linked: they tend to be inherited together, because a crossover is less likely to land in the short stretch between them. The closer, the stronger the linkage; the farther apart, the more likely recombination separates them. Test crosses measure recombination frequency and estimate genetic distance.
\[r = \frac{\text{number of recombinant offspring}}{\text{total offspring}}, \qquad 0\% \le r \le 50\%\]

\(r = 0\%\): complete linkage, always inherited together.
\(r = 50\%\): behaves as unlinked (different chromosomes or far apart). 50% is the ceiling because that is what independent assortment alone produces.

Linkage disequilibrium (LD) is central from Lecture 4 to Lecture 6, so understand it here. LD is the non-random association of alleles at different loci in a population: some combinations of alleles occur together more (or less) often than chance predicts. Loci close together tend to show high LD because recombination has had fewer chances to separate them. Recombination erodes LD over generations, but LD stays strong over the short distances relevant for most GWAS.
Detecting LD: compare the observed frequency of a haplotype (a specific combination of alleles at two or more loci on the same chromosome copy) with the frequency expected if the loci were independent. Observed ≈ expected → little or no LD. Observed ≠ expected → LD.

Worked example. Two biallelic loci: Locus 1 has A/a, Locus 2 has B/b. Frequencies: \(P(A) = 0.5\), \(P(B) = 0.4\).







Step
Calculation




Expected AB frequency if independent
\(P(A) \times P(B) = 0.5 \times 0.4 = \mathbf{0.20}\)


Observed AB haplotype frequency
From real data, say 0.30


Conclusion
0.30 ≠ 0.20 → the loci are in LD. The difference \(D = 0.30 - 0.20 = 0.10\) is the classic LD coefficient.




The measure \(D\) and the correlation-based \(r^2\) (Lecture 4–5) are standard ways to quantify LD; the slides use observed vs expected directly and \(r^2\) later.

  Strong LD, because 0.18 is much lower than 0.9
  No LD, because 0.18 equals 0.3 × 0.6
  Complete linkage, because both alleles are common
  LD cannot be judged without the recombination rate
  Expected under independence: 0.3 × 0.6 = 0.18. Observed equals expected, so there is no evidence of LD.

title: Lecture 3 — Recap, Mutations and Genetics
section: 3.8 First look at GWAS, and SNP arrays
text:
3.8 First look at GWAS, and SNP arrays
GWAS (genome-wide association study) searches the entire genome for variants associated with a trait or disease. Millions of SNPs are compared between individuals with different phenotypes; for each SNP you ask: is one allele more common among people with the trait?
Where LD comes in. A SNP that is significant in a GWAS is not necessarily the causal variant. Nearby variants are often in LD, so a significant SNP may simply be correlated with (“tag”) the real causal variant:
GWAS SNP  ⟷ (LD) ⟷  causal variant  ──▶  phenotype
A GWAS can show a strong association for “SNP A” even though “SNP B” does the biological work, just because A and B are inherited together.
SNP arrays (SNP chips) genotype hundreds of thousands to millions of known SNP positions at once. At a SNP such as rs12345 with alleles A or G, the array determines whether a person is AA, AG or GG.
Mechanism: the array holds many short DNA probes, each recognizing DNA with one particular allele. The person’s DNA is fragmented and allowed to hybridize (bind) to the probes; fluorescent signals show which probes bound.
DNA sample → fragment DNA → bind to SNP array → detect which probes light up → genotype
If both the “A signal” and the “G signal” light up at a position, the person is an AG heterozygote.

HWE gives the expected genotype frequencies in a population when allele frequencies stay constant across generations. The idealized assumptions: no selection, no new mutation, no migration, random mating, infinite population size. (The slides focus on the math rather than the full assumption list.)

title: Lecture 1 — The Biological Language of Molecular Epidemiology
text:
Molecular epidemiology is epidemiology that looks inside the body. Classical epidemiology links an exposure (smoking, diet, a drug) to a disease and treats everything in between as a black box. Molecular epidemiology opens that box. It measures DNA variants, RNA levels, proteins and metabolites across many people and asks how they relate to exposures and disease.
The course runs on one clinical example: a young patient with a heart attack, a father who had one too, and very high LDL cholesterol in the whole family. Following that family from DNA to protein to blood lipids to heart disease introduces almost every idea in the course, and the same LDLR/PCSK9 pathway comes back in Lectures 2, 3, 6 and 8.
The key intuition is that a molecule linked to a disease can play three roles. It can cause the disease, it can reflect a disease process that is already running, or it can simply be associated with it through something else. Most of the course is about telling these three apart.
This page covers the framing of the field, the LDL/PCSK9 example, the molecular measurement layers and biomarker types, and the DNA and protein structure you need for everything after this.

title: Lecture 1 — The Biological Language of Molecular Epidemiology
text:
1.1 What molecular epidemiology actually is
Classical epidemiology asks whether an exposure (smoking, diet, a drug) is associated with a disease outcome in a population and usually treats the biology in between as a black box. Molecular epidemiology opens that black box. It asks how changes at the molecular level (a DNA variant, an RNA transcript level, a protein concentration, a metabolite) cause, precede, accompany or result from disease. It studies the relationship in both directions: from molecule to disease, and from disease to molecule.
It is not the same discipline as biology. A molecular epidemiologist works with statistical evidence at the population level: associations, effect sizes, p-values. A molecular biologist provides the mechanistic, “definite” answers about how a change works in the cell. The two fields depend on each other. Statistical association points to candidates, and biological experiments confirm or explain the mechanism. The course frames this partnership as needing a shared vocabulary: you need to “talk biology” to read the molecular papers you build models around, and “talk bioinformatics/genetics” (variant nomenclature, databases, sequencing terms) to process the data.






ImportantCentral question of the field



Does a statistical association between a molecule and a disease reflect causality (the molecule contributes to causing the disease), or is it only correlated, a downstream consequence of disease, or a confounded association? This question runs through the whole course and is the explicit subject of Lecture 6 (Mendelian randomization).


Formal definition (the synthesis at the end of the lecture): molecular epidemiology studies how molecular variation across individuals relates to exposures, traits and disease in populations. In practice the field measures molecular variation across many individuals, links it to exposures, risk factors, disease, prognosis or treatment response, and then asks whether the associations are reproducible, predictive, mechanistically informative and potentially causal.

section: 1.2 The running example: cardiovascular disease, LDL and PCSK9
text:
1.2 The running example: cardiovascular disease, LDL and PCSK9
Why cardiovascular disease? Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is not one disease but a family of clinical phenotypes with overlapping biology:







Phenotype
What it is




Atherosclerotic CVD
Coronary artery disease, ischemic stroke, peripheral artery disease; all share atherosclerosis


Myocardial infarction (MI)
Acute interruption of coronary blood flow causing ischemic injury


Heart failure
Impaired pumping or filling; can follow ischemic injury, hypertension, cardiomyopathy and more


Stroke
Ischemic or hemorrhagic; ischemic stroke shares risk factors and mechanisms with coronary disease



Shared biological processes: atherosclerosis, thrombosis, inflammation, metabolic dysfunction and cardiac remodeling.
Two questions research keeps asking

Why does disease develop at all? Traditional risk factors (smoking, blood pressure, LDL cholesterol, diabetes), genetic susceptibility, environment and lifestyle, and the biological mechanisms connecting them to disease.
Why does disease differ between people who have it? Age of onset, severity, presentation (stable disease vs MI vs stroke vs heart failure), treatment response and prognosis.

Molecular measurements help with both: understanding mechanisms, identifying risk, improving prediction, finding biomarkers, discovering druggable targets and explaining variable treatment response. The goal is to separate molecules that are associated with disease, molecules that reflect ongoing disease, and molecules that participate in causing disease.
Background biology: cholesterol deposition. LDL (low-density lipoprotein) particles are macromolecules of protein and lipid that carry cholesterol in the blood. They form from larger VLDL (very low-density lipoprotein) particles, which the liver makes; VLDL is remodeled into LDL in the bloodstream. Most circulating LDL is cleared by the liver, prominently through the LDL receptor (LDLR). How much LDLR sits on the cell surface regulates how fast LDL is taken up. When blood LDL is high, more LDL enters the artery wall, gets trapped and starts atherosclerosis (plaque buildup).
The family case. A patient has a myocardial infarction young, with no explanation from age alone, and the father also had a premature MI, which suggests a hereditary risk factor. Lipid tests show the patient and several first-degree relatives all have markedly raised LDL cholesterol (LDL-C). Two conclusions: disease can be inherited, and high LDL-C seems linked to premature coronary heart disease. This motivates why you need DNA and heritability, mutations (changes in DNA), the DNA → gene → protein pathway, and how mutations make a protein work better or worse.
The molecular resolution. A mutation in the gene encoding the LDL receptor (LDLR) lowers its binding affinity for LDL. Liver cells take up LDL more slowly, circulating LDL rises and more LDL gets trapped in arteries.






WarningThis does not “solve” cardiovascular disease



Single-gene, strong-effect mutations like this are uncommon causes of CVD in the population. Most CVD comes from many small-effect variants plus lifestyle and environment. Finding the mechanism is still valuable: it identifies a druggable target (the LDLR/PCSK9 pathway) and teaches us LDLR’s normal function.


The LDLR–PCSK9 pathway. PCSK9 (Proprotein Convertase Subtilisin/Kexin type 9) is a protein that promotes degradation of the LDL receptor. More LDLR would clear more LDL-C, but drugs that increase expression of a target are hard to make, while drugs that decrease synthesis or block a protein are much easier. So drugs target PCSK9 and reduce its activity. That leaves more LDLR available and lowers LDL-C.
PCSK9 ──promotes degradation of──▶ LDLR ──clears──▶ LDL-C ──▶ atherosclerosis ──▶ CHD
   ▲
   └── drugs block or reduce PCSK9  ⇒  more LDLR  ⇒  lower LDL-C
This single pathway (LDLR–PCSK9–LDL-C) anchors gene regulation (L2), siRNA and antibody drugs (L3), Mendelian randomization (L6) and protein MR (L8). Know it well.

  It raises PCSK9 so that LDL receptors are built faster on liver cells
  It lowers PCSK9 activity, so fewer LDL receptors are degraded
  It replaces PCSK9 with LDL receptors taken up from the blood
  It turns PCSK9 into LDL so less cholesterol reaches the artery
  PCSK9 promotes LDLR degradation. Reducing PCSK9 (by blocking the protein or reducing its synthesis) leaves more LDLR on liver cells, so more LDL-C is cleared. Drugs that decrease or block are far easier to make than drugs that increase expression.

1.3 Molecular measurement layers
The course organizes “what can we measure” into layers with different properties. Memorize this table; Lecture 8 relies on the contrast between fixed DNA and dynamic RNA/protein.









Layer
What it tells us
Typical feature




DNA / genetic variation
Inherited predisposition

Proteins
Functional molecules and signaling

Metabolites

Highly responsive to physiology (changes fast)

Cellular composition and state
Context-dependent




Metabolites are small molecules produced, modified or consumed in biochemical reactions, for example glucose. Worked example of signaling: glucose signals insulin secretion, and insulin signals cells to take up glucose. Signaling means one molecule triggers a response that changes the behavior or output of another part of the system.
The causal chain used throughout the course

Genetic variation → RNA/gene expression → Protein amount or function → Metabolites/cellular processes → Cell behavior → Tissue and organ function → Clinical phenotype/disease

Two caveats, both important:

Changes can propagate down the chain, but the relationships are not always one-directional. Disease itself can change RNA, protein and metabolite levels, so an observed molecular change can be a consequence of disease.
Each level can therefore be a cause, an intermediate or a consequence depending on the case. This ambiguity is exactly why Lecture 6 introduces Mendelian randomization.

1.3b Biomarkers and their five roles
A biomarker is any measurable biological characteristic that provides information about a biological process, exposure, disease or treatment response. Being a biomarker does not imply being causal.








Biomarker role
Example




Exposure marker
Cotinine for tobacco exposure


Ongoing biological process
CRP (C-reactive protein) for systemic inflammation


Disease or tissue injury
Troponin for myocardial injury


Future risk
LDL-C for future atherosclerotic disease


Treatment response
Change in LDL-C after starting lipid-lowering therapy




Recognizing which of the five roles a biomarker plays in a study is a recurring skill in the course. Troponin comes back in Lecture 8 as the classic example of a useful predictor that is not causal.

  Exposure marker, like cotinine for tobacco smoke
  Marker of disease or tissue injury, released by damaged cells
  Marker of future risk, like LDL-C for atherosclerosis
  Marker of treatment response after lipid-lowering therapy
  Troponin is released when cardiomyocytes are damaged. It signals injury that has already happened. It is a good predictor but not a cause: lowering troponin would not treat the infarction (Lecture 8, Section 8.8).

title: Lecture 1 — The Biological Language of Molecular Epidemiology
text:
1.4 Central dogma and proteins
The central dogma describes the (mostly) one-way flow of genetic information in a cell: DNA → RNA → protein. DNA is the durable, inherited information store; RNA is a transient working copy transcribed from specific genes; proteins are the functional molecules translated from that RNA. Gene expression is the umbrella term for the two steps, transcription (DNA → RNA) and translation (RNA → protein). Lecture 2 covers both mechanically.
Proteins are long polymers (chains) of amino acids. There are 20 standard amino acids. A typical human protein is a few hundred amino acids long (median about 375 aa). Proteins are also called polypeptides; shorter chains of roughly 2–50 amino acids are called peptides.
Six functions of proteins, with the lecture’s examples







Function
Example




Catalyzing chemical reactions
Enzymes


Synthesizing and repairing DNA
DNA polymerases and repair enzymes


Transporting molecules
Hemoglobin carries oxygen


Receiving and sending chemical signals
LDL receptor as a receiver; insulin as the signal and the insulin receptor as the detector/responder


Responding to stimuli
Antibodies


Structural support
Collagen



Note the distinction between a signal molecule (insulin) and its receptor (insulin receptor).
Four levels of protein structure

Primary: the linear sequence of amino acids.
Secondary: regular local structures the chain folds into (alpha helices, beta sheets).
Tertiary: the overall 3D folded shape of one polypeptide chain.
Quaternary: several folded chains (subunits) assembled into one functional complex. Not every protein has this level.

Why this matters for genetics. The order of amino acids determines the 3D structure, and changing a single amino acid can change structure and therefore function. DNA holds the instructions for the amino acid sequence, so this is the direct link from a DNA mutation to a changed protein to a changed phenotype. Side note from the slides: other molecules, including drugs, can bind a protein and change its function without any change to DNA. That is how most pharmaceuticals work, as opposed to gene therapy.

  Primary structure, the order of amino acids
  Secondary structure, helices and sheets
  Tertiary structure, the fold of one chain
  Quaternary structure, several chains together
  Quaternary structure is the arrangement of multiple folded polypeptide chains into one complex. Tertiary is the 3D shape of a single chain. Not every protein has a quaternary level.

section: 1.4b DNA structure and complementary base pairing
text:
1.4b DNA structure and complementary base pairing
Genes, the basic physical and functional units of heredity, are made of DNA. DNA is a polymer of nucleotides; there are four types: A (adenine), C (cytosine), G (guanine), T (thymine). DNA normally forms a double helix: two strands wound around each other, held together by comparatively weak hydrogen bonds between complementary bases. Because these bonds are weak, the strands can be separated for replication and transcription without breaking the covalent backbone.
DNA as information. The order of nucleotides along a strand is the DNA sequence, and the information is encoded in that order. There is essentially no restriction on the order of A/C/G/T, which is why four building blocks can encode so much. For a sequence of 10 nucleotides there are \(4^{10} = 1\,048\,576\) possible sequences.
The slides tease the question how many letters are needed to specify an amino acid? Answer (Lecture 2): three nucleotides, a codon, specify one amino acid. Two letters would give only \(4^2 = 16\) combinations, too few for 20 amino acids; three give \(4^3 = 64\).
DNA as the unit of inheritance. To be hereditary material DNA must replicate. The mechanism is complementary base pairing: A pairs with T, C pairs with G. Because the pairing rule is fixed, each strand can act as a template for a new complementary strand. This is the physical basis of DNA replication.

  3′-ATGC-5′, the same letters in the same order
  3′-TACG-5′, pairing A with T and G with C
  3′-UACG-5′, since the copy uses uracil
  3′-GCAT-5′, the letters in reverse order
  A pairs with T and C pairs with G, and the strands are antiparallel. Under 5′-ATGC-3′ sits 3′-TACG-5′. Uracil only appears in RNA.

1.4c Chromosomes, mitosis and meiosis
Human DNA is organized into 23 different types of chromosomes, each containing many genes. Most human cells have 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs, one of each pair from the mother and one from the father. DNA replicates before cell division so each daughter cell gets a complete genome.










Mitosis
Meiosis

Genetically

None
Recombination shuffles alleles (Lecture 3)




The halving in meiosis lets two gametes combine at fertilization and restore 46 chromosomes. The shuffling during meiosis (recombination, Lecture 3) is why siblings differ genetically.

  It gives four identical cells with 23 chromosomes each
  It gives four different cells with 23 chromosomes each
  It gives two different cells with 46 chromosomes each
  Meiosis produces four genetically different gametes, each with half the chromosome number (23). Mitosis produces two identical cells with the full 46.

TipBH checklist for the exam






Sort the p-values from smallest to largest; write the rank \(i\) next to each.
Compute the threshold \(\frac{i}{m} Q\) for every rank.
Find the largest \(i\) with \(p_{(i)} \le \frac{i}{m} Q\). Call it \(k\). Do not stop at the first failure.
Everything with rank \(\le k\) is significant.
Adjusted p: compute \(p_{(i)} \cdot m / i\), then go from the bottom up taking the running minimum. Cap at 1.
Bonferroni for comparison: one threshold \(\alpha/m\) (or \(p \times m\)), same for all.
State the interpretation: BH controls the FDR (expected share of false hits among hits); Bonferroni controls the FWER (probability of any false hit).

title: Exam practice
text:
Written questions
Each question links to the section it comes from. Open the model answer only after you have tried.

🎯 Lecture 7: high-dimensional data






TipQ1. Explain why the ordinary t-test is problematic for omics data with few samples, and how the moderated t-statistic solves it.





Model answer. In omics data we measure thousands of features on few replicates, e.g. 3 vs 3 samples, giving only \(n_1 + n_2 - 2 = 4\) degrees of freedom per feature. Each feature’s variance \(s^2\) is estimated separately and is therefore very unstable. By chance some features get a tiny \(s^2\); since \(s^2\) is in the denominator of \(t\), they get huge t-values although the mean difference is small → false positives. Others get a randomly large \(s^2\), masking real effects → lost power. This instability affects every p-value and so also undermines the multiple-testing correction.
The moderated t (limma, empirical Bayes) shares information across all features: each variance is shrunk toward a common variance \(s_0^2\) estimated from the whole dataset, \(\tilde s^2 = (d_0 s_0^2 + d\, s^2)/(d_0 + d)\). With few replicates the prior weight \(d_0\) dominates and the shrinkage is strong; with many replicates the feature’s own variance dominates. Result: fewer false positives, more power, more reliable FDR-adjusted results. → 7.7–7.8









TipQ2. Define FWER and FDR. Which correction methods control each, and which is preferred for a miRNA microarray screen? Give reasons.





Model answer. FWER = P(at least one false positive among all tests), controlled by Bonferroni (\(p \le \alpha/m\)). FDR = the expected proportion of false positives among all tests called significant, E[FP / positives], controlled by Benjamini–Hochberg.
For omics screens FDR/BH is preferred: (1) with thousands of tests Bonferroni’s threshold is so small that most true effects are missed (0.05/955 ≈ 0.00005); (2) the analysis is exploratory, producing a shortlist where a controlled fraction of false leads is acceptable; (3) hits are validated afterwards in an independent cohort/method (miR-375 by qRT-PCR and in situ hybridization); (4) features are correlated, so the effective number of tests is smaller than \(m\) and Bonferroni is needlessly strict. → 7.11–7.14









TipQ3. The study tested 955 miRNAs. How many significant results would you expect at p < 0.05 if no miRNA truly differed? What is the Bonferroni threshold?





Model answer. \(955 \times 0.05 \approx 48\) false positives. Bonferroni: \(0.05/955 \approx 5.2 \times 10^{-5}\) (≈ 0.00005). With 955 independent null tests the chance of at least one false positive is \(1 - 0.95^{955} \approx 1\), so the cutoff itself must change. → 7.10









TipQ4. Describe the preprocessing of the microarray data. What does quantile normalization do and what does it assume?





Model answer. Observed signal = biological signal + technical noise (RNA extraction, labelling, hybridization, scanner, batch). Steps: (1) quality control; (2) background correction within each array with normexp, which models observed = signal (exponential) + background (normal) and estimates the true signal, giving positive values and better low-intensity estimates; (3) normalization between arrays with quantile normalization: rank the values in each array, average across arrays at each rank, replace each value by its rank mean, so all arrays get an identical distribution while keeping each array’s internal order; (4) average replicate probes (4–8 spots) per miRNA. Assumption of quantile normalization: the overall expression distribution should be the same in every sample, so distribution differences are technical. → 7.4–7.5









TipQ5. The authors clustered the samples on miRNA expression, found clusters M1 and M2, and then reported 141 miRNAs differentially expressed between M1 and M2. Comment critically.





Model answer. This is circular reasoning: the clusters were defined from the same miRNA data that was then tested. Clustering produces groups that differ in the clustering variables almost by construction, so significant differences are expected even in pure noise and the p-values are inflated. The differences are not independent evidence. Valid alternatives: test the cluster–clinical associations (grade, Ki67, chromosome 14 gain, which used other data), validate the clusters in an independent cohort, or use methods that account for the selection. → 7.16b









TipQ6. What does log₂FC = 1.5 mean? And why log-transform expression data at all?





Model answer. \(2^{1.5} \approx 2.83\): expression is about 2.8 times higher in the first group. log₂FC = 0 means no change, +1 twice as high, −1 half as high. Log₂ transformation makes the distribution more symmetric and reduces the influence of very large raw values; on the log scale, fold changes become differences. → 7.9









TipQ7. Five patients had both a primary tumour and a liver metastasis. Why were only their primary tumours used in the tumour vs normal comparison?





Model answer. Two samples from the same patient are not independent. Including both would double-weight those patients and violate the independence assumption of the test, biasing variance estimates and p-values. → 7.9b





🎓 Lectures 1–3: biology and genetics






TipQ18. Compare germline and somatic mutations.





Model answer. Germline: arise in egg/sperm, present in every cell, heritable, detected in blood/saliva, cause inherited disorders and hereditary cancer syndromes. Somatic: acquired during life in non-reproductive cells, confined to the tissue/tumour, not heritable, need a biopsy of the tissue, drive cancers and benign tumours (e.g. AML, detected by targeted deep sequencing and VAF). → 3.4









TipQ19. Read this (made-up) variant: NM_000999.3(GENEX):c.451C>T, p.Arg151Trp, rs123456789. What would p.Arg151Ter, p.Arg151= and c.451del mean?





Model answer. In the reference transcript NM_000999, version 3 (NM_ = mRNA/coding reference), c. position 451 of the coding DNA has C replaced by T. At the protein level (p.) arginine 151 becomes tryptophan: a single-base substitution that changes the amino acid, i.e. a missense variant (codon 151 spans c.451–453, so c.451 is its first base). rs123456789 would be its dbSNP identifier, the same across genome builds, whereas genomic positions (g., on an NC_ chromosome reference) differ between GRCh37 and GRCh38. p.Arg151Ter (also written p.Arg151*): the codon becomes a stop codon, a nonsense variant. p.Arg151=: the amino acid is unchanged, a silent variant. c.451del: one base deleted, which shifts the reading frame, a frameshift (written e.g. p.Arg151fs). → 2.4, 3.3b–3.3c









TipQ20. Compare miRNA and siRNA.





Model answer. miRNA: ~22 nt, genome-encoded, binds targets imperfectly, inhibits translation or promotes degradation, regulates many mRNAs (why it is widely dysregulated in cancer). siRNA: ~21–23 nt, from double-stranded RNA, binds with near-perfect complementarity, cleaves one specific mRNA, used as designed drugs. → 3.2









TipQ21. Define linkage, recombination frequency and linkage disequilibrium. How is LD detected?





Model answer. Linkage: loci close on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together. Recombination frequency \(r\) = recombinant offspring / total, 0% (complete linkage) to 50% (unlinked). LD: non-random association of alleles at different loci in a population. Detected by comparing observed haplotype frequency with the expected product of allele frequencies (e.g. expected AB = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.20); a difference indicates LD. Quantified with \(r^2\) (> 0.8 very strong; < 0.01 treated as independent). → 3.7





📌 Lecture 1: biomarkers






TipQ22. Give the five categories of biomarker with an example each. Is a biomarker causal?





Model answer. Exposure (cotinine for tobacco), biological process (CRP for inflammation), disease/tissue injury (troponin for myocardial injury), future risk (LDL-C for atherosclerosis), treatment response (LDL-C change on lipid-lowering therapy). Being a biomarker does not imply causality. → 1.3b





📌 Lecture 8: proteomics






TipQ25. How do you prevent and correct batch effects in a large proteomics study?





Model answer. Batch = plate, reagent lot, run, day, instrument, operator. Prevent (design): randomize samples across plates, balance cases and controls, technical replicates across plates, common reference samples on every plate. Detect: boxplots by plate, PCA, clustering, controls, replicates. Correct (analysis): normalization across plates/batches (incl. reference-sample normalization), adjust for plate/run or include batch as a covariate. Also consider pre-analytical variation (fasting, time to centrifugation, freeze–thaw, hemolysis) that may differ systematically between cases and controls. → 8.6









TipQ26. Compare the three families of protein measurement technology.





Model answer. Antibody-based (ELISA, immunoassays, Western blot): targeted, quantitative with standards, clinical routine. Mass spectrometry: trypsin digestion → LC → electrospray → masses; detects isoforms, allows discovery; complex, dynamic-range problems, labelled peptides for calibration. High-throughput affinity (Olink, SomaScan): thousands of proteins in large cohorts (UKBB: ~50,000 people, ~3,000 proteins), relative abundance in NPX (log₂; 1 NPX = doubling). → 8.4–8.5
