title: Exam practice
text:
Written questions

❔ Lectures 4–6: GWAS and MR theory






TipQ9. Distinguish vertical and horizontal pleiotropy. Which one is a problem for MR and why?





Model answer. Vertical: the SNP affects the outcome through the exposure (SNP → PCSK9 → LDLR → LDL-C → CHD); this is the causal chain MR measures, not a problem. Horizontal: the SNP also affects the outcome through a pathway independent of the exposure (SNP → inflammation → CHD); this violates the exclusion restriction and biases the MR estimate, because part of the SNP–outcome association is wrongly attributed to the exposure. → 6.6









TipQ11. Why are genetic variants useful for causal inference? Compare MR with an RCT.





Model answer. Genotype is fixed at conception, so it precedes the disease: no reverse causation. Alleles are allocated randomly at meiosis, like treatment in an RCT, so they are (under the independence assumption) unrelated to confounders such as smoking. An allele that lowers LDL-C is a lifelong “natural trial” of lower LDL-C. MR is cheaper and possible where RCTs are not, but relies on the three instrument assumptions. → 6.3–6.4









TipQ13. What is population stratification and how is it handled in a GWAS?





Model answer. If allele frequencies and the phenotype both differ between ancestry groups, pooling them creates a spurious SNP–phenotype association even without any biological effect. Handling: restrict to genetically homogeneous ancestry groups; adjust for genetic principal components; use mixed models that account for relatedness (e.g. regenie); check the QQ plot and genomic inflation. → 4.9









TipQ16. List the Bradford Hill criteria.





Model answer. Strength, Consistency, Specificity, Temporality, Biological gradient (dose–response), Plausibility, Coherence, Experiment, Analogy. → 6.2





❔ Lecture 8: protein MR






TipQ23. What is a cis-pQTL vs a trans-pQTL, and why are cis-pQTLs preferred as MR instruments?





Model answer. A pQTL is a SNP associated with a protein’s abundance. cis: near the encoding gene (mechanisms: transcription, splicing, stability, secretion). trans: far away, > 500 kb or another chromosome (mechanisms: transcription factors, receptors, signalling). cis-pQTLs are preferred because the link to the protein is direct and there is less risk of horizontal pleiotropy; they still need all three MR assumptions. Protein MR: \(\beta_{MR} = \beta_{GO}/\beta_{GP}\). → 8.9–8.10









TipQ24. List challenges specific to protein MR.





Model answer. Horizontal pleiotropy (especially trans-pQTLs); assay binding artifacts (coding variants change the epitope, fake lower abundance); amount ≠ function (variants changing activity without abundance are invisible); LD creating false appearance of causality (different SNPs in LD for protein and disease), checked by colocalization; one pQTL affecting several proteins. → 8.11





❔ Lecture 9: two-sample MR theory and PRS






TipQ27. What makes MR “two-sample”, what data does it need, and which assumptions still apply?





Model answer. The SNP → exposure effects come from one GWAS and the SNP → outcome effects from another, in different people. It needs only summary statistics per instrument: rsID, effect allele (and other allele, EAF for harmonisation), β and SE for the exposure, β and SE for the outcome; no individual-level data. All three MR assumptions still apply (relevance, independence, exclusion restriction); two-sample MR adds practical requirements: the SNPs must be found in both GWAS, the alleles harmonised, and the two samples comparable (ancestry, sex, age) but not overlapping. → 9.1–9.2









TipQ30. Name four practical problems in two-sample MR and the direction of bias each causes.





Model answer. Weak instruments with non-overlapping samples → bias toward the null. Sample overlap (people in both GWAS) → bias toward the confounded observational estimate. Winner’s curse (SNP effects overestimated in the discovery GWAS that selected them) → β_GX too large → estimate too small (toward the null); corrected by estimating effects in an independent replication sample. Different populations → associations may not transport; direction unpredictable. Also: horizontal pleiotropy is still possible, so report sensitivity analyses. → 9.8









TipQ31. Why is a genetically predicted exposure not the same as an intervention effect?





Model answer. Genotype acts from conception, so MR estimates the effect of a lifelong difference in exposure; lifetime exposure builds risk. A treatment in adulthood changes the exposure for a shorter period, so its effect is usually smaller. MR is most reliable about the direction of a causal effect. → 9.7









TipQ32. Contrast a PRS with MR. How is a PRS calculated, and what data does it need?





Model answer. MR asks whether X causes Y (population level, a few valid instruments). A PRS asks who is at higher risk (individual level, many SNPs, weak and pleiotropic SNPs allowed). \(PRS_i = \sum_j G_{ij}\hat\beta_j\): allele dosage (0/1/2) times GWAS effect size, summed over SNPs. It needs a discovery (base) sample giving the β’s and an independent target sample with individual genotypes, phenotype and covariates; overlap between them inflates the apparent accuracy. → 9.9–9.11









TipQ33. How are SNPs selected for a PRS, and why can it include weak instruments?





Model answer. Classical clumping + thresholding (C+T, “pruning and thresholding”): keep the lead SNP per locus, include SNPs with P below a threshold, trying several thresholds and validating the choice out of sample. Alternatives from statistical learning: model the LD between SNPs instead of clumping, and use LASSO/ridge or Bayesian shrinkage with a train/test split, which pulls noisy large effects toward zero (counters winner’s curse). Weak SNPs are allowed because a PRS only needs to predict: each adds a little signal, like weak learners; validity as a causal instrument is not required. → 9.12









TipQ34. What does a PRS value mean, and how do you evaluate whether it is useful?





Model answer. A PRS has no unit; it is a relative, roughly normally distributed measure and does not translate directly into a probability of disease. It is usually less predictive than age, sex or SBP. Evaluate: discrimination (AUC; does it rise when the PRS is added?), calibration (do predicted risks match observed?), and added prediction: compare age + sex + smoking + SBP with the same model + PRS (incremental R² or AUC). A strong OR per SD does not guarantee good screening; reclassification measures are more clinically relevant, and accuracy drops in ancestries unlike the discovery GWAS. → 9.13

Written questions






TipQ8. State the three assumptions of Mendelian randomization and give a threat to each.





Model answer. 1. Relevance: the variant is robustly associated with the exposure (genome-wide significant). Threat: weak instruments, which bias and destabilize the estimate. 2. Independence: the variant is not associated with confounders of the exposure–outcome relationship. Threats: population stratification, assortative mating, selection effects. 3. Exclusion restriction: the variant affects the outcome only through the exposure. Threat: horizontal pleiotropy (another pathway, e.g. SNP → inflammation → CHD). → 6.5









TipQ10. Explain the Wald ratio, IVW, weighted median and MR-Egger. When would you trust a causal conclusion?





Model answer. Wald ratio (one instrument): \(\beta_{\text{outcome}}/\beta_{\text{exposure}}\), change in outcome per genetically predicted unit of exposure (log-odds for binary outcomes). IVW: weighted regression of β-outcome on β-exposure through the origin = precision-weighted average of the Wald ratios; assumes all instruments valid. Weighted median: consistent if at least ~50% of the instrument weight is valid, so robust to a minority of bad instruments. MR-Egger: free intercept; a non-zero intercept indicates directional horizontal pleiotropy; less precise and more sensitive to weak instruments, relies on the InSIDE assumption. Trust grows when all methods point in the same direction, since their weaknesses differ. Always state the exposure unit and the direction. → 6.7–6.9









TipQ12. A Manhattan plot shows a tall peak with dozens of significant SNPs. Explain why, and what “lead SNP” and “locus” mean. Is the lead SNP causal?





Model answer. Nearby SNPs are correlated (in LD) because they are inherited together, so one causal variant makes all SNPs in LD with it look associated. The locus is the region containing the associated signal; the lead SNP is the one with the smallest p-value there. It is not necessarily causal: it may be a proxy, and the causal variant may not even be on the array. Ways forward: conditional analysis, credible sets, functional annotation, protein folding models, pQTL evidence, experiments (knock-in mice). → 4.8, 5.3–5.4









TipQ14. Why is the genome-wide significance threshold 5×10⁻⁸? Does p < 5×10⁻⁸ mean the SNP matters?





Model answer. About 1 million independent tests: \(0.05/10^6 = 5 \times 10^{-8}\) (Bonferroni); at 0.05 you would get ~50,000 false positives. Significance means statistical robustness only. It says nothing about effect size (huge samples make tiny effects significant), causality or public-health relevance (rs11591147 has a big effect but is rare, 1.5%). → 4.7, 4.10









TipQ15. What must you always know when using GWAS summary statistics?





Model answer. Which allele is the effect allele (A1/EA); whether β is an OR or log(OR) for binary outcomes; the scale of the phenotype (log? SD units?); the genome build (GRCh37/hg19 vs GRCh38). When combining datasets also check SNP coverage, allele/strand alignment and ancestry of the LD reference panel. rsIDs help avoid mismatches. → 4.6, 5.6









TipQ28. Describe the six steps of a two-sample MR analysis. Where is the difficulty?





Model answer. (1) Select instruments for X: P < 5×10⁻⁸, sufficiently strong (F = (β/SE)² > 10), independent (LD clumping). (2) Look up the same SNPs in the outcome GWAS (use a proxy SNP in high LD if one is missing). (3) Harmonise alleles so both β’s refer to the same effect allele; flip the sign when swapped, handle strand, exclude ambiguous palindromic SNPs. (4) Estimate: Wald ratio per SNP, IVW over SNPs. (5) Sensitivity analyses: weighted median, MR-Egger (intercept), leave-one-out, heterogeneity. (6) Interpret, stating the exposure unit. The slides stress that the difficulty lies in steps 1–3. → 9.3–9.6









TipQ29. Exposure GWAS: effect allele A, other allele G, β = +0.08. Outcome GWAS: effect allele G, other allele A, β = −0.03. Harmonise and compute the Wald ratio. What happens if you forget?





Model answer. The outcome β is per G; per A it is +0.03. Wald ratio = 0.03 / 0.08 = 0.375: Y increases 0.375 units per unit of genetically predicted X. Without harmonising: −0.03 / 0.08 = −0.375, the opposite conclusion (X looks protective). → 9.5

title: Computer exercises: concepts
text:
The two computer exercises turn Lectures 4–6 into a working pipeline. Exercise 1 goes from genotypes to a GWAS and then reduces many significant SNPs to a few independent signals, first with individual-level data and then with published summary statistics. Exercise 2 uses those independent signals as instruments in a Mendelian randomization of LDL-C on coronary artery disease.
This page is not a solution to the exercises. It uses its own made-up tables and simulated data so you can practise the concepts and interpretations: what each QC filter does, how to read association output, how clumping works, how to align alleles between two files, and how to read IVW, MR-Egger and weighted median results. Then do the exercises yourself with the course data.

section: A2. Why rare variants are hard for single-SNP regression
text:
A2. Why rare variants are hard for single-SNP regression
The standard error of the per-allele β shrinks with the number of carriers. For a continuous phenotype with residual SD \(\sigma\) and \(n\) people, approximately
\[\text{SE}(\hat\beta) \approx \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{2\,n\,\text{MAF}\,(1-\text{MAF})}}\]
because the variance of the 0/1/2 dosage under HWE is \(2\,\text{MAF}(1-\text{MAF})\). With MAF = 0.001 in 2,500 people you expect only about 5 carriers, so β rests on a handful of people: huge SE, low power, and sensitivity to a single genotyping error.





Approximate SE of β (phenotype SD = 1) against MAF, for 2,500 and 100,000 people. SE explodes as MAF approaches zero; the dashed line marks MAF = 0.01.

A4. Significant SNP, lead SNP, independent signal







Term
What it is




Significant SNP
Any SNP with p below the threshold (e.g. 5×10⁻⁸). Many can come from one causal variant


Lead SNP
The strongest (smallest p) SNP in a region; the representative of a peak


Independent signal
What is left after clumping: lead SNPs with r² below the threshold (e.g. < 0.01) to each other


Causal SNP
The variant that actually changes biology. It may be a lead SNP, a SNP in LD with it, or not genotyped at all



Does distance predict LD? Only roughly. LD tends to decay with distance, but recombination hotspots, allele frequencies and population history make the relationship very noisy. Always compute r².

title: Computer exercises: concepts
text:
A5. Manual LD clumping
The algorithm used in the exercises:

Among the remaining significant SNPs, pick the smallest p-value as a lead SNP.
Compute r² between it and every other remaining significant SNP.
Remove all SNPs with r² ≥ 0.01 (they are “the same signal”).
Keep the lead as one signal and repeat from step 1 until nothing is left.

Practise on invented tables. The drill gives a new table each time.












TipCommon mistakes in clumping






Starting from a SNP that is not the strongest remaining one.
Comparing with SNPs that have already been removed.
Using a threshold in the wrong direction (remove r² ≥ 0.01, keep r² < 0.01).
Concluding that the lead SNPs are causal. They are the strongest statistical signals. A simulated phenotype, where the causal SNPs are known, is exactly the situation where you can check this.

C2. Reading an MR analysis: a simulated example
Simulated data, not the course data: 30 independent instruments with a true causal effect of 0.5 (log-odds of the outcome per unit exposure). Four instruments also have a direct effect on the outcome (horizontal pleiotropy).





Simulated MR scatter. Orange points are the four pleiotropic instruments. IVW (green) is forced through the origin; MR-Egger (orange, dashed) has a free intercept; the dotted line shows the true effect 0.5.







MR estimates for the simulated data (true causal effect = 0.5)


Method
Estimate
p-value




IVW

0.335

0.031
0.004

How to read it

IVW uses all instruments and assumes they are all valid. With positive pleiotropy in a few SNPs it is pulled upward.
Weighted median is robust as long as at least ~50% of the weight comes from valid instruments. Here it should be closer to 0.5.
MR-Egger’s intercept estimates the average pleiotropic effect. Here it is clearly non-zero, signalling directional pleiotropy. The Egger slope is meant to be the pleiotropy-adjusted estimate, but in this simulation it lands well below the truth: with only four pleiotropic SNPs among 30, the free intercept over-corrects. Egger is imprecise and relies on its own assumption (InSIDE), so treat its slope as a sensitivity check, not the answer.
Agreement in direction across the three methods supports a causal effect; the size of the estimates should be interpreted with the exposure unit in mind (6.9).


  Consistent evidence of a positive effect, no sign of directional pleiotropy
  The Egger intercept shows strong pleiotropy, so IVW is invalid
  The methods disagree in direction, so no conclusion is possible
  The effect is negative, since Egger’s slope is smaller than IVW
  All three estimates are positive and similar, and the Egger intercept is close to zero and non-significant. That is the triangulation pattern that strengthens a causal interpretation. The Egger p-value is larger simply because Egger is less precise.


  A strong and robust causal effect, since IVW is the main method
  IVW is probably driven by pleiotropic instruments; be cautious
  The weighted median is wrong because its p-value is not significant
  Egger’s intercept confirms that the instruments are all valid
  The robust method (weighted median) finds almost nothing, and the Egger intercept indicates directional pleiotropy. IVW, which assumes all instruments are valid, is then likely biased. Look for outlying instruments and do not claim causality from IVW alone.


  Nothing, because IVW only uses βexposure
  Those five points land on the wrong side of the line
  All points move closer to the origin by the same amount
  The Wald ratios of those five SNPs become exactly zero
  A swapped allele gives the outcome β the wrong sign, so those SNPs point in the opposite direction from the rest. They pull IVW toward zero and can create a spurious Egger intercept. This is why allele alignment comes before any MR estimate.

title: About the content
text:
The app is built from a study guide (sta520-study-app-guide_1.md) synthesized from the course’s lecture slides (PDF/PPTX), expanded with textbook-level background explanations. The background prose is written independently from general molecular biology, genetics and biostatistics knowledge. title: Glossary
text:
A–C

Additive model

The standard GWAS model: phenotype regressed on allele dosage (0/1/2), so each extra copy adds the same effect β. Additive/dominant/recessive describe the genotype–phenotype relationship, not the allele. L4 §4.4

Allele

An alternative version (DNA sequence) at a particular locus. L3 §3.6 · L4 §4.2

Allele frequency / MAF

How common an allele is in a population. MAF (minor allele frequency) is the frequency of the less common allele. L4 §4.2

Alternative splicing

One gene’s transcript spliced into several different mRNA/protein variants; one reason proteins are not 1-to-1 with genes. L8 §8.1

AML (acute myeloid leukemia)

A non-solid blood cancer driven by somatic mutations in bone marrow stem cells; the course’s example of somatic mutation diagnostics with NGS and VAF. L3 §3.4

Antibody-based assay

ELISA, clinical immunoassays, Western blot: an antibody binds its target protein; targeted and quantitative with calibration standards. L8 §8.4

Assay binding artifact

A coding variant changes the protein’s structure so the antibody/aptamer binds worse, giving a falsely low measured level. A protein-MR pitfall. L8 §8.11

Assortative mating

Non-random mate choice related to a trait; a threat to the MR independence assumption. L6 §6.5

AUC (area under the ROC curve)

Probability that a random case gets a higher predicted risk than a random control; 0.5 = chance, 1 = perfect. Used to ask whether a PRS adds discrimination. L9 §9.13

Background correction (normexp)

Within-array correction modelling observed intensity as exponential signal + normal background noise; gives positive values and better low-intensity estimates. L7 §7.5

Batch effect

A shared technical artifact among samples processed together (plate, reagent lot, run, day, instrument, operator). Prevent by randomizing/balancing; correct by normalization or batch covariates. L7 §7.4 · L8 §8.6

Benjamini–Hochberg (BH)

FDR-controlling procedure: sort p-values, find the largest k with p₍ₖ₎ ≤ (k/m)Q, call ranks 1…k significant. Adjusted p = running minimum of p₍ᵢ₎·m/i from the bottom. L7 §7.13 · L7 §7.13b

Biomarker

Any measurable biological characteristic informative about a process, exposure, disease or treatment response. Five roles: exposure, process, disease/injury, future risk, treatment response. Not necessarily causal. L1 §1.3b

Bonferroni correction

FWER control: reject if p ≤ α/m (p_adj = p × m). Valid under any dependence but very strict for large m. L7 §7.12 · L4 §4.7

Bradford Hill criteria

Strength, Consistency, Specificity, Temporality, Biological gradient, Plausibility, Coherence, Experiment, Analogy. L6 §6.2

Calibration

Agreement between predicted and observed risks (predicted 10% → about 10% get the disease). L9 §9.13

Central dogma

The flow of genetic information DNA → RNA → protein. L1 §1.4 · L2 §2.2

Chromosomal alterations

Large-scale changes: deletion, duplication, inversion, insertion, translocation. L2 §2.4b

Circular reasoning (double dipping)

Using the same data to define groups (e.g. clusters) and then to test differences between those groups; inflates significance. L7 §7.16b

cis-pQTL

A pQTL located near the gene encoding the protein; direct interpretation, preferred MR instrument. L8 §8.9 · L4 §4.10

Clumping + thresholding (C+T)

Classical PRS method (“pruning and thresholding”): keep one lead SNP per locus, include SNPs with P below a threshold. L9 §9.12

Codon

Three nucleotides specifying one amino acid (or stop). 64 codons for 20 amino acids. L1 §1.4b · L2 §2.3

Coding strand

The non-template DNA strand; same sequence as the mRNA with T instead of U. L2 §2.2

Colocalization

Checks whether a pQTL and a disease GWAS signal at one locus share the same causal variant by comparing their association patterns across the region. L8 §8.11

Complementary base pairing

A pairs with T (U in RNA), C pairs with G; the basis of replication and transcription. L1 §1.4b

Conditional analysis

Adding the lead SNP as a covariate and retesting other SNPs to find independent signals. L5 §5.4

Confounding

A third factor affecting both exposure and outcome (e.g. smoking → LDL-C and CHD). L6 §6.4 · L8 §8.8

Covariates (in GWAS)

Age, sex, BMI, genetic PCs, technical variables (batch, center). β is conditional on them. L4 §4.5

Credible set

A set of candidate causal SNPs chosen from association strength and LD structure. L5 §5.4

title: Glossary
text:
D–H

dbSNP / rs number

NCBI database of short variants; each gets a stable rs identifier (e.g. rs137852912 = PCSK9 D374Y). L3 §3.3c

Discovery (base) and target sample

In PRS analysis: the discovery GWAS supplies the β estimates; the independent target sample supplies genotypes, phenotype and covariates. L9 §9.11

Dominant / recessive allele

Dominant affects the phenotype with at least one copy; recessive only with two. L3 §3.6

Empirical Bayes / variance shrinkage

Sharing information across features: each variance is pulled toward a common value. Basis of limma’s moderated t. L7 §7.7 · L7 §7.8

Exclusion restriction

MR assumption 3: the variant affects the outcome only through the exposure. Broken by horizontal pleiotropy. L6 §6.5

F-statistic (instrument strength)

F = (β_GX / SE)² for one SNP; F < 10 marks a weak instrument. L9 §9.3

FDR (false discovery rate)

Expected proportion of false positives among the tests called significant. Controlled by BH. L7 §7.11

Frameshift

An indel whose length is not a multiple of 3, shifting all downstream codons. L2 §2.4b

FWER (family-wise error rate)

Probability of at least one false positive among all tests. Controlled by Bonferroni. L7 §7.11

Gain / loss of function (GoF / LoF)

A mutation making the protein work better (D374Y in PCSK9) or worse (p.Tyr142*, p.Arg97del). L3 §3.3

GalNAc / ASGPR

Sugar linked to the siRNA in Leqvio that binds ASGPR receptors on hepatocytes: an “address label” to the liver. L3 §3.2b

Gene expression

Transcription + translation; regulated at chromatin, transcription, RNA processing, mRNA degradation and post-translational levels. L1 §1.4 · L2 §2.3

Genome build (GRCh37/hg19, GRCh38)

Versions of the human reference genome; the same variant has different coordinates in different builds. HG18/HG19 are older names. L3 §3.3c · L4 §4.6

Genome-wide significance

p < 5 × 10⁻⁸ ≈ 0.05 / 1,000,000. L4 §4.7

Genotype / phenotype

Genotype = the alleles an individual carries; phenotype = the observable trait. L3 §3.6

Genotyping

Determining alleles at already-known variant positions (TaqMan, SNP arrays), as opposed to sequencing. L3 §3.5 · L3 §3.8

Germline mutation

Arises in germ cells, present in every cell, heritable. L3 §3.4

GWAS

Genome-wide association study: one regression per SNP for ~1 million SNPs. Gives associations, not causality. L3 §3.8 · L4 §4.6 · L5 §5.2

Haplotype

A combination of alleles at two or more loci on the same chromosome copy. L3 §3.7

Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium (HWE)

With allele frequencies p and q: P(AA) = p², P(Aa) = 2pq, P(aa) = q². Deviations are a genotyping QC check. L3 §3.9 · L4 §4.2

Harmonisation

Aligning alleles so the exposure and outcome β refer to the same effect allele (flip the sign when swapped; handle strand and palindromic SNPs). L9 §9.5

HGVS nomenclature

Standard variant notation: reference (NM_ mRNA, NC_ genomic, NP_ protein) + coordinate type (c., g., p.) + change (e.g. c.1120G>T, p.Asp374Tyr). L3 §3.3b

Homozygous / heterozygous

Two identical alleles (BB, bb) vs two different alleles (Bb). L3 §3.6

Horizontal pleiotropy

A variant affects the outcome through a pathway independent of the exposure; violates the exclusion restriction. L6 §6.6 · L8 §8.11

title: Glossary
text:
I–M

Imputation

Predicting genotypes at unmeasured SNPs from measured SNPs using LD and a reference panel. L6 §6.1

In-frame indel

An insertion/deletion of a multiple of 3 nucleotides; frame preserved (e.g. PCSK9 p.Arg97del). L2 §2.4b

Independence (MR assumption)

MR assumption 2: the variant is not associated with confounders. Threats: population stratification, assortative mating, selection. L6 §6.5

Instrumental variable

A variable affecting the exposure but related to the outcome only through it; genetic variants are natural instruments. L6 §6.3

IVW (inverse-variance weighted) MR

Weighted regression of β-outcome on β-exposure through the origin = weighted average of Wald ratios. L6 §6.7 · L9 §9.6

LD clumping

Reducing each locus to one approximately independent lead SNP (e.g. r² < 0.01); done before MR. L5 §5.4b · L9 §9.3

LDL / LDLR

Low-density lipoprotein carries cholesterol; the LDL receptor on hepatocytes clears it. L1 §1.2

Lead SNP

The SNP with the smallest p-value in a locus; not necessarily causal. L4 §4.8 · L5 §5.3

limma / moderated t-statistic

R package using empirical Bayes variance shrinkage to give stable t-statistics with few samples. L7 §7.7

Linkage

Loci close on the same chromosome are inherited together. L3 §3.7

Linkage disequilibrium (LD)

Non-random association of alleles at different loci in a population; observed ≠ expected haplotype frequency. Measured by r² (or D). L3 §3.7 · L4 §4.8

Locus

A position on a chromosome; in GWAS, a region containing associated variants (one Manhattan peak). L3 §3.6 · L4 §4.10

Log₂ fold change

log₂(group 1 / group 2): 0 = no change, +1 = 2× higher, −1 = 2× lower. L7 §7.9

Manhattan plot

−log₁₀(p) against genomic position; peaks show where associations are, not which variant is causal. L4 §4.7

Mass spectrometry

Trypsin digestion → liquid chromatography → electrospray ionization → mass measurement; detects isoforms, allows discovery. L8 §8.4

Meiosis / mitosis

Meiosis: 4 different gametes with 23 chromosomes. Mitosis: 2 identical cells with 46. L1 §1.4c

Mendel’s laws

Dominance, Segregation, Independent Assortment (broken by linkage). L3 §3.6

Mendelian randomization (MR)

Using genetic variants as instruments to estimate causal effects of an exposure on an outcome. L6 §6.3 · L8 §8.10

Metabolite

A small molecule produced, modified or consumed in biochemical reactions (e.g. glucose). L1 §1.3

miRNA (microRNA)

~22 nt genome-encoded non-coding RNA; binds targets imperfectly and regulates many mRNAs. L3 §3.2 · L7 §7.2

Missense / nonsense / silent

Substitution giving a different amino acid / a premature stop / the same amino acid. L2 §2.4

Monoclonal antibody

An engineered protein binding one specific target; Repatha and Praluent bind PCSK9 protein. L3 §3.2b

MR-Egger

MR regression with a free intercept; a non-zero intercept signals directional horizontal pleiotropy. Less precise than IVW. L6 §6.8

mRNA / rRNA / tRNA

Messenger RNA carries the code; ribosomal RNA builds ribosomes; transfer RNA brings amino acids. L2 §2.1

Multivariable MR

MR with several related exposures in one model (e.g. apoB, LDL-C and remnant cholesterol), so each causal estimate is adjusted for the others. L9 §9.14

Mutation

A change in the DNA sequence (L2’s definition). Point mutations (silent, missense, nonsense), indels (frameshift, in-frame) and chromosomal alterations; germline or somatic; gain or loss of function. In practice largely interchangeable with variant, which is the more neutral term. L2 §2.4 · L2 §2.4b · L3 §3.3 · L3 §3.4

Multiple testing

Many tests at α = 0.05 give many false positives (955 × 0.05 ≈ 48; 1,000,000 × 0.05 = 50,000). L7 §7.10 · L4 §4.7

title: Glossary
text:
N–R

NGS (next-generation sequencing)

Massively parallel sequencing: fast and cheap, short reads (~50–300 nt). L3 §3.5

NPX (Normalized Protein eXpression)

Olink/SomaScan relative abundance on a log₂ scale; 1 NPX = a doubling. L8 §8.5

Olink / SomaScan

High-throughput affinity proteomics platforms for large cohorts. L8 §8.4

OncomiR

A miRNA that promotes cancer (e.g. miR-1246, miR-663a). L7 §7.2 · L7 §7.16

Odds ratio (per allele)

OR = exp(β) from logistic regression; β = −0.16 → OR 0.85 (one copy), 0.73 (two copies). L4 §4.3

Palindromic SNP

A/T or C/G SNP whose complement is the same allele pair, so strand cannot be read from the letters; resolved by allele frequency or excluded. L9 §9.5

PCR

Polymerase chain reaction: in vitro amplification of a DNA region using heat-stable Taq polymerase and primers. L2 §2.6

PCSK9

Protein promoting LDLR degradation; the course’s running drug-target example. L1 §1.2 · L3 §3.3 · L8 §8.12

Polygenic risk score (PRS)

Sum over SNPs of allele dosage × GWAS effect size for one individual; a relative measure of genetic liability, not a probability. L9 §9.10

Population stratification

Allele frequency and phenotype both differ between ancestry groups, creating spurious associations. L4 §4.9

Pre-analytical variation

Variation before the assay: fasting, time of day, tube type, time to centrifugation, storage, freeze–thaw, hemolysis. L8 §8.6

Primer

Short DNA sequence where synthesis starts; DNA polymerase needs one, RNA polymerase does not. L2 §2.2 · L2 §2.6

Protein structure (4 levels)

Primary (sequence), secondary (helices, sheets), tertiary (3D fold), quaternary (several chains). L1 §1.4

Proteome

All proteins in a sample; more dynamic and complex than the genome. L8 §8.1

Proxy SNP

A SNP in very strong LD (r² ≈ 1) that stands in for a missing SNP. L6 §6.1

Post-translational modification (PTM)

Chemical changes after translation, e.g. phosphorylation, glycosylation, cleavage. L8 §8.1

pQTL (protein quantitative trait locus)

A SNP associated with a protein’s abundance; cis (near the gene) or trans (> 500 kb away). L8 §8.9

PWAS

Proteome-wide association study: one regression per protein. L8 §8.7

QQ plot

Observed vs expected p-values; deviation can mean confounding/batch or high polygenicity. L4 §4.7

QTL

Quantitative trait locus: a region where genetic variation is associated with a quantitative trait (expression, protein, metabolite). L4 §4.10

Quantile normalization

Between-array normalization making all distributions identical while keeping within-array order. L7 §7.5

r² (LD)

Squared genotype correlation between two SNPs: > 0.8 very strong, > 0.5 moderate–strong, < 0.1 weak, ≈ 0 independent. L4 §4.8 · L5 §5.4b

Recombination / recombination frequency

Exchange of segments between homologous chromosomes in meiosis; r = recombinants / total, 0–50%. L3 §3.7

Relevance (MR assumption)

MR assumption 1: the variant is strongly associated with the exposure; threat: weak instruments. L6 §6.5

Remnant cholesterol (TRL/remnant-C)

Cholesterol in triglyceride-rich lipoproteins and their partly lipolysed remnants; computed as non-HDL-C − LDL-C. L9 §9.14

title: Glossary
text:
S–Z

Sample overlap

Individuals present in both GWAS (MR) or in both discovery and target data (PRS); biases MR toward the observational estimate and inflates PRS accuracy. L9 §9.8 · L9 §9.11

Sanger sequencing

The original sequencing method: accurate, lower throughput. L3 §3.5

siRNA

~21–23 nt RNA from double-stranded RNA; near-perfect match cleaves one target mRNA (Leqvio). L3 §3.2

SNP / SNV

Single nucleotide variant; called a SNP (polymorphism) when common in the population. L2 §2.4 · L4 §4.2

SNP array

Chip with allele-specific probes genotyping up to millions of known SNPs by hybridization and fluorescence. L3 §3.8

snRNA

Small nuclear RNA involved in splicing. L3 §3.1

Somatic mutation

Acquired during life, confined to a tissue, not heritable. L3 §3.4

Summary statistics

Per-SNP GWAS results (SNP, CHR, BP, A1, A2, EAF, β, SE, P, N) with no individual-level data. L4 §4.6 · L9 §9.2

Supervised / unsupervised analysis

Using predefined group labels (differential expression) vs finding groups from the data (clustering). L7 §7.6

Taq polymerase

Heat-stable DNA polymerase used in PCR. L2 §2.6

Template strand

The DNA strand read by RNA polymerase (non-coding strand). L2 §2.2

Transcription / translation

DNA → mRNA (in the nucleus) / mRNA → protein at the ribosome (initiation, elongation, termination at UAA, UAG, UGA). L2 §2.2 · L2 §2.3

Transcription factor

Protein binding DNA to raise or lower transcription. L2 §2.2

trans-pQTL

pQTL far (> 500 kb or other chromosome) from the encoding gene; indirect, more pleiotropy risk. L8 §8.9

Troponin

Released by damaged heart muscle; a marker of injury, predictive but not causal. L1 §1.3b · L8 §8.8

Two-sample MR

MR with SNP → exposure and SNP → outcome effects taken from two different GWAS; needs only summary statistics. L9 §9.1

VAF (variant allele frequency)

Fraction of reads/cells in one patient’s sample carrying a mutation. L3 §3.4

Variant (genetic variant)

Any place where a person’s DNA sequence differs from the reference genome (or from other people). The neutral umbrella term: it covers SNVs/SNPs, small insertions and deletions (indels) and larger structural changes, whether common or rare, harmful or harmless. It is the word used in HGVS notation, dbSNP (rs numbers), GWAS and MR (“genetic variant as instrument”). Mutation usually stresses the change event or a rare, often disease-related change; polymorphism (the P in SNP) a variant that is common in the population. L2 §2.4 · L3 §3.3b · L3 §3.3c · L4 §4.2 · L6 §6.3

Vertical pleiotropy

The variant affects the outcome through the exposure itself; not a problem for MR. L6 §6.6

Wald ratio

MR estimate with one instrument: β_outcome / β_exposure (β_GO / β_GP in protein MR). L6 §6.7 · L8 §8.10 · L9 §9.6

Weak instrument

A SNP explaining little of the exposure (F < 10); biases MR toward the null (no overlap) or toward the confounded estimate (overlap). L9 §9.8

Weighted median

MR estimator valid if at least ~50% of instrument weight is valid. L6 §6.8

Winner’s curse

Effect sizes of newly discovered variants tend to be overestimated in the GWAS that found them; in MR this biases toward the null. L9 §9.8

z-score

(x − mean) / SD; puts proteins on a common scale, β per SD. L8 §8.6 · L8 §8.7

title: Martin’s key concepts
text:
On 2 October the course published Martin’s key concepts, a list of 20 concepts for the GWAS, Mendelian randomization (MR) and proteomics part of the course (Lectures 4–6, 8 and 9). When the lecture pages were written this list did not exist, so the material is spread across many sections and some concepts only got a sentence or two.
This page collects the list into 20 short modules, in the list’s own order. Each module gives an exam-ready definition you can say in one or two sentences, the common confusion to avoid, a quick check, and links to the lecture sections that go deeper. Three concepts that were thin in the lectures get more space here: additive, dominant and recessive models (K.4), colocalization (K.19) and biomarker vs causal protein (K.20).
Mark each module Reviewed or Confident as you go. The status is saved in this browser and counted on the dashboard under 🔑.

title: Martin’s key concepts
text:
K.1 SNP (single-nucleotide polymorphism)






TipSay it in one sentence



A SNP is a single base position in the genome where people in a population carry different nucleotides (alleles), for example some have C and others T; each SNP has an identifier such as an rs number from dbSNP.



Usually biallelic: two alleles, often called the reference/other and the effect allele in GWAS files.
“Polymorphism” traditionally means common enough to be a normal variant in the population (often minor allele frequency ≥ 1%). A rare change in one family is usually called a variant or mutation.
SNPs are what SNP arrays genotype and what GWAS tests, one at a time.

Don’t confuse: a SNP is a position with variation in the population; an allele is one of the possible bases at that position; a genotype is the pair of alleles one person carries.
Deeper: 3.3c dbSNP and rs numbers · 4.2 SNPs, alleles, MAF

  A deletion of one gene that only some people carry
  A single base position where alleles differ between people
  A mutation that arises in a tumour but not in the germline
  The one allele that a person has at a given position
  A SNP is a position with variation across the population. One person’s pair of alleles at it is their genotype.

title: Martin’s key concepts
text:
K.2 Genotype and allele dosage (0/1/2)






TipSay it in one sentence



The genotype is the pair of alleles a person carries at a SNP; the allele dosage codes it as the number of copies of the effect allele, 0, 1 or 2, which is the X variable in the GWAS regression.






Genotype (effect allele = T)
CC
CT

Dosage
0
1
2





Imputed SNPs give an expected dosage between 0 and 2 (for example 1.7), because the genotype is predicted with uncertainty.
The dosage only means something once you know which allele is counted. Swap the effect allele and every dosage becomes 2 − dosage, and β changes sign.

Don’t confuse: dosage counts the effect allele, which is not always the minor allele or the “risk” allele.
Deeper: 4.4 The additive model · A3 Reading association output

  2, because the person has two copies of an allele
  1, because G is the other allele at this SNP
  0, because the person has no copies of A
  It cannot be coded without knowing the MAF
  Dosage counts copies of the effect allele. GG has zero A alleles, so dosage = 0.

title: Martin’s key concepts
text:
K.3 Minor allele frequency (MAF)






TipSay it in one sentence



The minor allele frequency is the frequency of the less common allele at a SNP in a given population, so it is always between 0 and 0.5.



Computed from genotype counts: each heterozygote contributes one copy, each homozygote two. With \(n_{AA}, n_{Aa}, n_{aa}\): \(f_a = (2n_{aa} + n_{Aa}) / (2N)\).
Low MAF means low power: few people carry the allele, so β is estimated with a large SE. Rare variants are why GWAS QC often filters on MAF.
MAF is population-specific. The minor allele in Europeans can be the major allele in another ancestry, which matters when combining datasets (seminar question on GLGC vs 1000 Genomes).

Don’t confuse: MAF is not the same as the effect allele frequency (EAF). If the effect allele is the major allele, EAF = 1 − MAF.
Deeper: 4.2 SNPs, alleles, MAF and genotype frequencies · 3.9 Hardy–Weinberg

  0.04, the share of people who are TT
  0.36, the share of people who carry a T
  0.20, the share of all alleles that are T
  0.80, the share of all alleles that are C
  T alleles = 2 × 40 + 320 = 400 out of 2,000 alleles = 0.20. T is the less common allele, so MAF = 0.20.

K.4 Additive, dominant and recessive models






TipSay it in one sentence



The genetic model says how the genotype is coded in the regression: additive counts copies (0/1/2, each copy adds the same effect), dominant compares carriers with non-carriers (0/1/1), and recessive compares two copies with the rest (0/0/1).



Coding of the same SNP under the three models (effect allele = T)










Model
CC

What β means

Recessive (T recessive)

Mean phenotype by genotype under each model, with the same effect of 1 unit. Additive: a straight line through 0, 1, 2. Dominant: the heterozygote already looks like TT. Recessive: only TT differs.




Why GWAS use the additive model (Lecture 4, “Worth noting 2”): you test a million SNPs and do not know each one’s true pattern. The additive model is the simple default; it has reasonable power even when the true pattern is dominant or recessive, and it uses one degree of freedom. Dominant and recessive models are useful when you study one specific SNP or gene in depth.
Don’t confuse: dominance describes the genotype–phenotype relationship, not the allele. The same allele can act dominant for one phenotype and recessive for another (Lecture 4).
Deeper: 4.4 The additive model · 3.6 Mendelian genetics

  Each extra copy of T is compared with one fewer copy
  People with at least one T against people with no T
  People with two copies of T against everyone else
  Heterozygotes against both kinds of homozygote
  Recessive coding is 0/0/1: only TT is coded 1, so β is the difference between TT and the CC + CT group.


  Dominant, since one copy has the full effect
  Additive, since each copy adds one unit
  Recessive, since only TT differs from CC
  None, since the heterozygote should lie halfway
  CT already has the same mean as TT, so one copy is enough: a dominant pattern (0/1/1). An additive pattern would give about 4.0, 4.5, 5.0 or 4, 5, 6.

title: Martin’s key concepts
text:
K.5 Genome-wide association study (GWAS)






TipSay it in one sentence



A GWAS tests each of roughly a million SNPs across the genome, one at a time, for association with a phenotype, using a regression of the phenotype on allele dosage adjusted for covariates such as age, sex and genetic principal components.



Hypothesis-free: no candidate gene is chosen in advance.
Output: one β, SE and p per SNP (summary statistics, K.11), shown as a Manhattan plot (position vs −log₁₀ p) and checked with a QQ plot.
Continuous phenotype → linear regression (β = mean difference per allele); binary → logistic regression (β = log-odds per allele, OR = e^β).
A GWAS finds associations. The top SNP is usually a tag in LD with the causal variant, and the association can still be confounded (population structure).

Don’t confuse: GWAS finds loci, not genes or mechanisms. Going from a hit to biology needs fine-mapping, QTL data, colocalization, MR or experiments.
Deeper: 4.6 The GWAS scan · 4.9 Population structure · 4.10 From hit to biology · 5.2 The full GWAS pipeline

  To increase the number of SNPs that can be tested
  To adjust for ancestry differences that can confound
  To convert the additive model into a dominant one
  To remove SNPs that are in strong LD with each other
  If allele frequencies and the phenotype both differ between ancestry groups, SNPs look associated because of ancestry. The PCs capture ancestry and remove that confounding.

text:
K.6 Effect size, standard error and p-value






TipSay it in one sentence



The effect size β is the estimated change in the phenotype per copy of the effect allele (log-odds for a binary outcome), the standard error says how precisely β is estimated, and the p-value measures the evidence against β = 0, based on \(z = \beta / SE\).



Example. β = 0.05 SD per allele, SE = 0.008.



Step
Value




z = β / SE
0.05 / 0.008 = 6.25


Two-sided p
≈ 4 × 10⁻¹⁰, below 5 × 10⁻⁸


95% CI
0.05 ± 1.96 × 0.008 = 0.034 to 0.066





SE shrinks with larger sample size, higher MAF and lower phenotype variance. That is why a tiny β can have a tiny p in a large GWAS.
Binary outcome: β is a log(OR). OR per allele = e^β; for two copies under the additive model, OR = e^(2β).
p measures evidence, not importance. A highly significant SNP can explain almost none of the phenotype variance.

Don’t confuse: a small p-value does not mean a large effect. Compare β (and its units) to judge size.
Deeper: 4.3 Phenotype types and the per-allele effect · 4.4 β, SE and p




  SNP 2 has a larger effect on the phenotype
  SNP 2 has a higher MAF or a larger sample
  SNP 2 lies closer to the gene it regulates
  SNP 2 was tested with the dominant model
  SE depends on sample size, allele frequency and phenotype variance. With β the same, a smaller SE comes from more information: more people or more carriers of the allele.

title: Martin’s key concepts
text:
K.7 Genome-wide significance






TipSay it in one sentence



Genome-wide significance is the conventional threshold p < 5 × 10⁻⁸ for a GWAS hit; it is a Bonferroni correction of α = 0.05 for about one million independent common-variant tests in the genome.


\[\frac{0.05}{1\,000\,000} = 5 \times 10^{-8}\]

“Independent” is the key word: there are many more SNPs than that, but because of LD neighbouring SNPs are correlated, so the effective number of independent tests in European-ancestry genomes is about one million.
It controls the family-wise error rate: the chance of even one false positive across the whole scan is about 5%.
SNPs with 5 × 10⁻⁸ < p < 10⁻⁵ are sometimes called “suggestive”.

Don’t confuse: passing the threshold does not make a SNP causal, and failing it does not mean “no effect”; it may mean too little power.
Deeper: 4.7 Multiple testing, Manhattan and QQ plots · 7.11 FWER vs FDR · 7.12 Bonferroni

  It is the p-value of the strongest SNP in the first GWAS
  0.05 divided by about a million independent tests
  0.05 divided by the total number of SNPs on an array
  It is the FDR level that Benjamini–Hochberg gives
  Bonferroni: α / m with m ≈ 10⁶ independent tests, after accounting for LD. It is a FWER threshold, not an FDR threshold.

title: Martin’s key concepts
text:
K.8 Linkage disequilibrium (LD; r²)






TipSay it in one sentence



Linkage disequilibrium is the non-random association between alleles at nearby SNPs in a population, so knowing one SNP’s allele tells you something about the other’s; r² is the squared correlation between the two SNPs’ allele dosages, from 0 (independent) to 1 (perfect proxy).



LD exists because nearby SNPs are inherited together: recombination between them is rare, so the haplotypes they sat on are preserved over generations.
r² = 1: one SNP perfectly predicts the other, so they give the same GWAS signal. r² ≈ 0: independent.
LD is population-specific. Compute it in a reference panel that matches the ancestry of the GWAS (for example the European part of 1000 Genomes).
LD generally decays with distance, but physical distance is not LD: two close SNPs can have low r², and LD blocks vary in size.

Don’t confuse: linkage is about co-inheritance within families (recombination frequency); LD is the correlation of alleles across a population.
Deeper: 3.7 Linkage, recombination and LD · 4.8 Lead SNP and r² · 5.4b r² bands




  A similar association, since B almost copies A
  No association, because only one SNP can be causal
  An association in the opposite direction from A
  An association only if B lies inside a gene’s exon
  With r² = 0.95, B’s alleles nearly predict A’s, so B shows almost the same signal. That is why GWAS hits appear as towers of correlated SNPs.

title: Martin’s key concepts
section: K.9 Lead SNP and GWAS locus
text:
K.9 Lead SNP and GWAS locus






TipSay it in one sentence



A GWAS locus is a genomic region with a significant association signal, usually many correlated SNPs; the lead SNP is the SNP with the smallest p-value in that locus and is used to represent it.



A locus is defined around the lead SNP, by a distance window (for example ± 500 kb) and/or by LD with the lead SNP.
The lead SNP is the best statistical tag, not necessarily the causal variant. The causal variant can be any SNP in strong LD with it, or one that was not genotyped at all.
One locus can contain more than one independent signal (conditional analysis or clumping can reveal a secondary signal).

Don’t confuse: “lead SNP” (strongest p in the region) ≠ “causal SNP” (the variant that changes the biology) ≠ “nearest gene” (often assumed, not proven).
Deeper: 4.8 Lead SNP and r² · 4.10 Locus, lead SNP, QTLs · 5.4 Finding the causal SNP

  Because the lead SNP is always in a non-coding region
  Because SNPs in strong LD with it give nearly the same p
  Because the lead SNP is chosen by its position in the gene
  Because causal variants never reach genome-wide significance
  Many SNPs in high LD carry almost the same signal, and the smallest p among them can be partly chance or better genotyping. The causal variant may be another SNP in LD or an unmeasured one.

title: Martin’s key concepts
section: K.10 LD clumping and independent genetic signals
text:
K.10 LD clumping and independent genetic signals






TipSay it in one sentence



LD clumping reduces a list of significant SNPs to independent signals: take the most significant SNP, remove all SNPs within a window that are in LD with it above an r² threshold, and repeat with the next most significant remaining SNP.



The algorithm







Step
Action




1
Sort significant SNPs by p, smallest first


2
Take the top SNP as an index SNP


3
Remove SNPs within the window (for example 1,000 kb) with r² above the threshold (for example 0.01–0.1)


4
Repeat with the next remaining SNP until none are left





Why: correlated SNPs carry the same information. For MR you need independent instruments, otherwise the same signal is counted several times and the SE is too small. For PRS clumping avoids double-counting.
Choices matter: a wider window compares more SNP pairs (slower, catches long-range LD, leaves fewer SNPs); a lower r² threshold removes more SNPs (stricter independence).
More SNPs can survive clumping than there are causal variants: two weakly correlated tags of one causal variant can both pass a lenient threshold, and SNPs outside the window are never compared.

Don’t confuse: “independent” (low r² between the kept SNPs) is not “causal”. Each clump still represents a region.
Deeper: 5.4b r² bands and LD clumping · A5 Manual LD clumping · Seminar S.1 and S.5

  Clumping makes every instrument genome-wide significant
  Correlated SNPs would count one signal several times
  Clumping removes the need to harmonise the alleles
  IVW can only handle one SNP per chromosome at most
  IVW treats each SNP as independent evidence. SNPs in LD repeat the same signal, so the estimate gets falsely precise.

title: Martin’s key concepts
text:
K.11 GWAS summary statistics






TipSay it in one sentence



GWAS summary statistics are the per-SNP results of a GWAS (SNP ID, chromosome, position, effect and other allele, allele frequency, β, SE, p and N) with no individual-level data, which is why they can be shared publicly and reused, for example in two-sample MR or PRS.



Before using them, check four things: which allele is the effect allele, whether β is OR or log(OR), the scale of the phenotype (SD units? log?), and the genome build (hg19/GRCh37 vs hg38/GRCh38).
LD cannot be computed from summary statistics: they have no genotypes per person. Use a reference panel with matching ancestry.
Two-sample MR needs two sets: one for the exposure, one for the outcome, matched on SNP and allele.

Don’t confuse: summary statistics are per SNP, not per person. You cannot rerun the regression with new covariates from them.
Deeper: 4.6 Summary statistics · 5.5 LD with summary statistics · 9.2 The data you need

  Reading off the β and p of a given SNP
  Finding SNPs below p = 5 × 10⁻⁸
  Estimating r² between two SNPs for clumping
  Converting a log-odds β into an odds ratio
  r² needs the genotypes of individuals. Summary statistics have none, so LD comes from a reference panel such as 1000 Genomes.

title: Martin’s key concepts
text:
K.12 Instrumental variable (IV)






TipSay it in one sentence



An instrumental variable is a variable that shifts the exposure, shares no causes with the outcome, and affects the outcome only through the exposure; it lets you estimate a causal effect even when the exposure–outcome relationship is confounded.


   Z (instrument) ───▶ X (exposure) ───▶ Y (outcome)
                          ▲                ▲
                          └──── U (confounders) ┘

The idea comes from econometrics. The classic example is the randomization in an RCT: the coin flip shifts treatment and is independent of everything else.
In MR the instrument is a genetic variant: alleles are allocated at conception, before the exposure and the disease, and independently of most lifestyle confounders.

Don’t confuse: an IV is not a confounder or a covariate to adjust for. Its job is to give variation in the exposure that confounders do not touch.
Deeper: 6.3 Genetic variants as instruments · 6.4 Why we need MR: confounding

  The outcome measured at the end of follow-up
  The confounders recorded at the baseline visit
  The random allocation to treatment or control
  The treatment the participant actually took
  Allocation shifts the treatment received and is independent of confounders, just like an allele in MR. The treatment actually taken is the exposure.

title: Martin’s key concepts
text:
K.13 Mendelian randomization (MR)






TipSay it in one sentence



Mendelian randomization uses genetic variants associated with an exposure as instrumental variables to estimate the causal effect of the exposure on an outcome, exploiting that alleles are randomly allocated at conception, which limits confounding and rules out reverse causation.



“Nature’s randomized trial”: people who inherited exposure-raising alleles are, on average, like people who were randomized to a slightly higher exposure for life.
One-sample MR: exposure and outcome in the same people. Two-sample MR: SNP–exposure and SNP–outcome effects from two different GWAS, using only summary statistics.
The answer is the effect per unit of genetically predicted exposure, which is lifelong and usually small; it is not the same as the effect of a drug given in middle age.

Don’t confuse: MR is only as good as its three assumptions (K.14). A significant MR estimate with a pleiotropic instrument is not causal evidence.
Deeper: 6.4 Why we need MR · 9.1 Two-sample MR · 9.7 Interpreting an MR estimate

  Because the outcome GWAS is always run before the exposure GWAS
  Because MR uses only SNPs located inside the exposure’s gene
  Because the disease cannot change the inherited genotype
  Because the Wald ratio is always positive for causal effects
  The genotype is fixed at conception. Disease can change measured biomarkers but not the alleles, so the arrow cannot run from outcome to instrument.

title: Martin’s key concepts
text:
K.14 The three MR assumptions






TipSay it in one sentence



A valid MR instrument must be (1) relevant: robustly associated with the exposure; (2) independent: not associated with confounders of the exposure–outcome relationship; and (3) satisfy the exclusion restriction: affect the outcome only through the exposure.












#
Assumption
How you check it
Typical threat




1
Relevance
p < 5 × 10⁻⁸ in the exposure GWAS; F-statistic > 10
Weak instruments


2
Independence
Cannot be proven; adjust for ancestry, check associations with known confounders
Population stratification, assortative mating, selection


3
Exclusion restriction
Cannot be proven; biology of the gene, MR-Egger intercept, weighted median, outlier tests
Horizontal pleiotropy





Only assumption 1 can be tested directly. Assumptions 2 and 3 are made plausible, never proven, which is why MR uses several sensitivity analyses.

Don’t confuse: “the SNP is associated with the outcome” is not an assumption. That is what MR tests, and it is only interesting if the three assumptions hold.
Deeper: 6.5 The three MR assumptions · 6.8 Sensitivity analyses · 9.3 F-statistic

  Relevance, from the SNP–exposure association
  Independence, from the SNP–outcome association
  Exclusion restriction, from the MR-Egger slope
  None of them, since all three are untestable
  Relevance is visible in the exposure GWAS (p-value, F-statistic). Independence and exclusion restriction involve unmeasured paths and can only be made plausible.

title: Martin’s key concepts
text:
K.15 Horizontal vs vertical pleiotropy






TipSay it in one sentence



Pleiotropy is one variant affecting several traits. It is vertical when the variant affects the outcome through the exposure (fine for MR), and horizontal when it affects the outcome through a separate pathway that bypasses the exposure (violates the exclusion restriction).


Vertical (OK):     SNP ──▶ LDL-C ──▶ atherosclerosis ──▶ CHD

Horizontal (bad):  SNP ──▶ LDL-C ──────────────────────▶ CHD
                     └──▶ inflammation ────────────────▶ CHD

Horizontal pleiotropy shows up as instruments whose Wald ratios disagree with the rest, an MR-Egger intercept away from zero, or IVW and weighted median giving different answers.
trans-pQTLs and SNPs in genes with many functions are the usual suspects. cis instruments in the exposure’s own gene reduce the risk.

Don’t confuse: vertical pleiotropy is not a problem to remove. It is the causal chain MR is designed to detect.
Deeper: 6.6 Pleiotropy · 6.8 MR-Egger and weighted median · 9.8 Pleiotropy and pitfalls

  Vertical pleiotropy, which does not bias the estimate
  Horizontal pleiotropy, which can bias the estimate
  A weak-instrument problem under the relevance assumption
  Reverse causation from stroke to blood pressure
  The SNP reaches stroke through BMI, a path that does not go through blood pressure. That is horizontal pleiotropy and breaks the exclusion restriction.

title: Martin’s key concepts
section: K.16 Wald ratio and inverse-variance weighted (IVW) MR
text:
K.16 Wald ratio and inverse-variance weighted (IVW) MR






TipSay it in one sentence



With one instrument the causal estimate is the Wald ratio, the SNP’s effect on the outcome divided by its effect on the exposure; with several independent instruments the IVW estimate is a precision-weighted average of the Wald ratios, equal to a weighted regression of β-outcome on β-exposure through the origin.


\[\hat\beta_{\text{Wald}} = \frac{\beta_{\text{SNP}\to Y}}{\beta_{\text{SNP}\to X}}, \qquad SE_{\text{Wald}} \approx \frac{SE_{\text{SNP}\to Y}}{|\beta_{\text{SNP}\to X}|}\]
\[\hat\beta_{\text{IVW}} = \frac{\sum_j \beta_{X_j}\beta_{Y_j}/SE_{Y_j}^2}{\sum_j \beta_{X_j}^2/SE_{Y_j}^2}\]

Example. Three clumped SNPs (exposure in mmol/L, outcome log-odds).



SNP
β exposure
β outcome
SE outcome
Wald ratio

0.10

0.50


2

IVW numerator = (0.20·0.10 + 0.10·0.06)/0.0004 + 0.30·0.12/0.0009 = 65 + 40 = 105. Denominator = (0.04 + 0.01)/0.0004 + 0.09/0.0009 = 125 + 100 = 225. IVW = 105/225 ≈ 0.47 log-odds per mmol/L, OR ≈ e^0.47 ≈ 1.6.


Before computing: harmonise the alleles so both β refer to the same effect allele, and for a binary outcome use log(OR).
Through the origin = assumes no horizontal pleiotropy (zero exposure effect → zero outcome effect). MR-Egger frees the intercept to test that.

Don’t confuse: the Wald ratio is per unit of the exposure’s scale. An exposure in SD units and one in mmol/L give different numbers for the same biology.
Deeper: 6.7 The Wald ratio and IVW · 9.5 Harmonisation · 9.6 Wald ratio and IVW







  Because the exposure GWAS centres all β values at zero
  Because a SNP with no exposure effect should have no outcome effect
  Because weighting by precision removes the intercept term
  Because it makes the estimate robust to pleiotropic SNPs
  Under the exclusion restriction the only way a SNP affects the outcome is through the exposure, so zero on X must give zero on Y. A non-zero intercept (MR-Egger) suggests directional pleiotropy.

title: Martin’s key concepts
text:
K.17 Proteomics and protein abundance






TipSay it in one sentence



Proteomics is the large-scale measurement of the proteins in a sample (the proteome); most platforms measure protein abundance, the amount or concentration of each protein, often as a relative value such as Olink’s log₂-scale NPX, not its activity.



Why proteins: they do the work in cells, change with disease, diet, drugs and age, and are the targets of most drugs.
Why it is hard: plasma protein concentrations span about 10 orders of magnitude, so a few abundant proteins (albumin, immunoglobulins) dominate; one gene can give several proteoforms (isoforms, post-translational modifications).
Platforms: affinity-based (Olink, SomaScan: antibodies or aptamers, thousands of proteins, relative units) and mass spectrometry (peptides, can see isoforms and give absolute amounts with internal standards).
NPX is relative and log₂: +1 NPX = twice as much of that protein in that sample. It cannot be compared between different proteins.

Don’t confuse: abundance ≠ function. A variant can change what a protein does without changing how much there is, and an affinity assay can miss a form it does not bind.
Deeper: 8.1 Why study the proteome · 8.4 Three technology families · 8.5 Units and NPX · 8.13 Reading: comparing eight platforms

  Sample B has about four times as much protein X
  Sample B has 2 units/mL more protein X than sample A
  Sample B has more protein X than any protein in sample A
  Sample B’s protein X is more biologically active
  NPX is log₂, so a difference of 2 = 2² = 4-fold for the same protein. It says nothing about other proteins or about activity.

title: Martin’s key concepts
text:
K.18 pQTLs: cis-pQTL and trans-pQTL






TipSay it in one sentence



A pQTL (protein quantitative trait locus) is a genetic variant associated with the abundance of a protein; it is cis when it lies near the gene that encodes the protein (commonly within 500 kb–1 Mb) and trans when it lies far away or on another chromosome.












cis-pQTL
trans-pQTL




Location
Near the protein’s own gene
Far away (> 500 kb) or another chromosome


Likely mechanism
Direct: transcription, splicing, stability, secretion of that protein
Indirect: transcription factors, receptors, pathways


As MR instrument
Preferred: clear biology, less pleiotropy
Higher risk of horizontal pleiotropy





Found with a GWAS that has the protein level as the phenotype: protein = β₀ + β₁ × dosage + ε.
Caution: a coding (missense) cis variant can change the epitope an antibody or aptamer binds and fake a pQTL: lower measured signal, unchanged amount.

Don’t confuse: cis is defined relative to the protein’s gene, not relative to any gene. A SNP next to gene A that changes protein B is trans for B.
Deeper: 8.9 pQTLs · 8.10 Protein MR · 8.11 Challenges of protein MR

  A cis-pQTL, a good candidate MR instrument
  A trans-pQTL, with a high risk of pleiotropy
  A cis-pQTL, which proves ABC causes disease
  An eQTL, since it is near a gene’s promoter
  Near the protein’s own gene → cis. cis-pQTLs are preferred instruments for protein MR, but the three MR assumptions and colocalization still need checking.

title: Martin’s key concepts
text:
K.19 Colocalization






TipSay it in one sentence



Colocalization asks whether two association signals in the same region, for example a pQTL for a protein and a GWAS hit for a disease, are driven by the same causal variant, rather than by two different variants that happen to be close together and in LD.


The logic from the slides (Lecture 8): compare the pattern of association across the region for the protein and for the disease. If one shared variant drives both, SNPs in LD with it produce the same shape of signal for both traits: the same SNPs are strongest, and the association weakens in step as LD with the shared variant falls.





Simulated regional association plots. Left: one shared causal variant, so the protein and disease peaks have the same shape and the same top SNP. Right: two different causal variants 60 kb apart; the peaks overlap in the region but do not line up.




Why MR alone is not enough: if SNP A raises the protein and a different SNP B in LD with A raises disease risk through another mechanism, an MR using A will still find a “protein → disease” effect. That is LD confounding. Colocalization checks for it.






NoteBeyond the slides: the formal coloc method





The widely used Bayesian method (the R package coloc) compares five hypotheses for a region: H0 no association with either trait, H1 only trait 1, H2 only trait 2, H3 both traits but different causal variants, H4 both traits and one shared causal variant. It reports a posterior probability for each, and PP.H4 above about 0.8 is often taken as evidence of colocalization. It needs only summary statistics for both traits in the region. The slides describe the idea; this formal version is background, not course material.



Don’t confuse: “both signals are in the same locus” is not colocalization. Two causal variants 50 kb apart can sit in one locus with overlapping towers of association.
Deeper: 8.11 Challenges of protein MR (colocalization) · 8.12 From association to mechanism

  The protein causes the disease, since the signals overlap
  Two different causal variants drive the two signals
  The pQTL must be a trans-pQTL for the protein P
  The disease GWAS must be confounded by ancestry
  If one variant drove both, the same SNPs would be strongest for both traits. Mismatched peaks point to distinct causal variants, so an MR through P here may reflect LD, not causation.

title: Martin’s key concepts
text:
K.20 Biomarker vs causal protein






TipSay it in one sentence



A biomarker is a measurable molecule that indicates a state or risk (it can be a cause, a consequence or just a correlate of disease), whereas a causal protein is one where changing its level or activity changes disease risk, which is what you need for a drug target.












Biomarker
Causal protein




Question
Does it predict or reflect disease?
Does changing it change disease?


Evidence
Association, prediction (AUC), reproducibility
MR with cis-pQTLs, colocalization, experiments, trials


Useful for
Diagnosis, prognosis, risk prediction, monitoring treatment
Drug targets, understanding mechanism


Example type
Troponin after heart damage: excellent marker, consequence not cause
A protein whose cis-pQTL predicts disease in MR and colocalizes





A protein associated with disease in a PWAS can be (1) a cause, (2) a consequence of disease (reverse causation), or (3) a correlate sharing a confounder (smoking, BMI, inflammation).
A good biomarker does not have to be causal; a causal protein is not always a good biomarker (it may vary little between people or be hard to measure).
The route from biomarker to causal protein (Lecture 8): association → pQTL → MR and colocalization → experiments (CRISPR, cell models, animal models).

Don’t confuse: “strongly associated” and “predictive” do not mean “causal”. Lowering a consequence-marker does not undo the disease.
Deeper: 1.3b Biomarkers and their five roles · 8.7 PWAS · 8.8 Association is still not causation · 8.12 From association to mechanism

  It causes heart attacks and should be a drug target
  It is a useful biomarker, but may not be causal
  It must have a strong cis-pQTL in the general population
  It proves that MR would find a causal effect on CHD
  Rising after the event suggests it is a consequence (like troponin). Prediction makes it a useful biomarker; causality needs MR, colocalization or experiments.

title: Lecture 2 — DNA, RNA and Protein
text:
Lecture 1 introduced the central dogma, DNA → RNA → protein, as a one-line idea. This lecture is the machinery behind that line: how a gene is copied into messenger RNA, how the ribosome reads that RNA three letters at a time, and how a protein comes out the other end.
Once you know how the machinery works, you can describe what happens when it goes wrong. A single changed letter can do nothing (a silent change), swap one amino acid (missense), or stop the protein early (nonsense). Inserting or deleting letters can shift how every following codon is read. These categories are the vocabulary for every mutation in the rest of the course, including the PCSK9 variant D374Y.
The key intuition is the reading frame: the ribosome reads mRNA in fixed groups of three. Most of the mutation rules follow from that one fact.
This page covers RNA vs DNA, transcription and strand terminology, translation and the genetic code, mutation types, the PCSK9 D374Y example and PCR. The strand-and-translate exercise at the bottom is the classic exam-style calculation.

2.2 Transcription, strands and directionality
Protein synthesis has two steps: transcription and translation. In transcription a gene (a defined stretch of DNA) is copied into mRNA; the mature mRNA is exported from the nucleus and translated in the cytoplasm.
Transcription factors are proteins that bind DNA and increase or decrease the rate of transcription. They are one of the main controls over which genes are “on” in which cell type.
Strand terminology (a frequent source of confusion, be precise):








Term
Also called
What it is




Template strand
Non-coding strand
The strand RNA polymerase reads and copies from


Coding strand
Non-template strand
Same sequence as the mRNA, with T instead of U


mRNA
Transcript
Made complementary to the template strand, so identical to the coding strand (U for T)









ImportantDirectionality rules (repeated across Lectures 2 and 3)




DNA and RNA are always synthesized 5′ → 3′: new nucleotides are added to the 3′ end.
The new RNA strand is antiparallel to the DNA template strand. Antiparallel orientation is what makes base pairing physically possible.
DNA polymerase needs a primer to start. RNA polymerase does not.

title: Lecture 2 — DNA, RNA and Protein
text:
2.3 Translation and the genetic code
Translation: the ribosome reads the code in the mRNA and builds a protein. It takes place at ribosomes. The genetic code maps three-nucleotide codons to amino acids and has three properties:







Property
Meaning




Universal
Essentially the same in all known life


Unambiguous
Each codon specifies exactly one amino acid


Redundant (degenerate)
Most amino acids have several codons (64 codons, 20 amino acids)



tRNA’s role: each tRNA carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon that base-pairs with the matching codon, delivering the right amino acid at the right moment.
Three stages of translation

Initiation: the ribosome assembles on the mRNA at the start codon (AUG, methionine).
Elongation: amino acids are added one at a time as the ribosome moves along, each linked to the growing chain.
Termination: at a stop codon. The three stop codons are UAA, UAG and UGA, given identically in Lectures 2 and 3. Memorize them.

Gene expression differs between cell types. Human cells have roughly 20,000 genes, but each cell type makes different proteins because different genes are expressed. Expression can be regulated at several stages:

chemical/structural modification of DNA or chromatin
transcription
post-transcriptional modification of RNA
mRNA degradation
post-translational modification of the protein

This is why having a gene and expressing it are different things, and why RNA and protein measurements depend on tissue and context (the layer table in Lecture 1).

  AUG, UAA, UGA
  UAA, UAG, UGA
  UAA, UAG, AUG
  UGA, UGG, UAG
  The stop codons are UAA, UAG and UGA. AUG is the start codon (methionine); UGG codes for tryptophan.

2.4b Mutations: indels and chromosomal changes
Indels (insertions and deletions) add or remove one or more nucleotides. The effect depends on how many, because the ribosome reads in fixed groups of three:








Type
Number of nucleotides
Effect




Frameshift
Not a multiple of 3
Every downstream codon is shifted; the rest of the protein is scrambled, often with an early stop


In-frame
A multiple of 3
Reading frame preserved; only the affected amino acid(s) are added or removed



Chromosomal alterations affect whole chromosome segments: deletion, duplication, inversion, insertion, translocation.

  A frameshift that scrambles all downstream amino acids
  A silent change that leaves the protein sequence intact
  One amino acid is lost but the reading frame is kept
  A premature stop codon at the site of the deletion
  Three nucleotides is one codon. The frame downstream is preserved, so the protein simply lacks one amino acid (in-frame deletion). PCSK9 c.290_292delGCC (p.Arg97del) in Lecture 3 is exactly this.

2.6 PCR: polymerase chain reaction
PCR amplifies (makes many copies of) a specific region of DNA in vitro (in a test tube). “Worth a Nobel Prize”: Kary Mullis won the 1993 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it.







Component
Role




Taq polymerase
A heat-stable DNA polymerase. It survives the repeated heating steps PCR needs, unlike most enzymes


Primers

PCR underlies many methods in this course: TaqMan SNP genotyping (Lecture 3) and amplifying a small region around a suspected mutation before sequencing in AML diagnostics (Lecture 3).

  Taq polymerase survives the repeated heating steps
  Taq polymerase copies RNA as well as DNA templates
  Taq polymerase reads the strand in the 3′ to 5′ direction
  PCR repeatedly heats the sample to separate the strands. Taq is heat-stable, so it survives every cycle. It still needs primers, which define the amplified region.

title: Lecture 4 — From SNP to GWAS
text:
A genome-wide association study (GWAS) is one simple regression repeated about a million times. For each SNP you count how many copies of one allele each person carries (0, 1 or 2), regress the phenotype on that count, and record the effect size, its standard error and a p-value. That is the whole method; everything else in this lecture is about doing it carefully and reading the output correctly.
For example, if each copy of an allele raises LDL cholesterol by 0.2 mmol/L on average, the regression slope is 0.2. For a disease outcome you use logistic regression instead, and the slope becomes a log odds ratio.
The intuition to hold on to: genetic effects are usually small compared with everything else that varies between people, but with enough people you can still detect them. Testing a million SNPs at once also means you need a much stricter p-value threshold, and a significant SNP tells you where to look, not what is causal.
This page covers allele and genotype frequencies, the additive model for continuous and binary outcomes, covariates, GWAS summary statistics, multiple testing, Manhattan and QQ plots, why hits come in clusters, population structure and the step from a hit to biology. This lecture is calculation-heavy: be able to redo every worked example with new numbers.

title: Lecture 4 — From SNP to GWAS
section: 4.1 Genotype → phenotype, and why association is not causation
text:
4.1 Genotype → phenotype, and why association is not causation
DNA variation can plausibly cause a phenotype (disease status, a biomarker level). The reverse is logically impossible: a phenotype or disease cannot change your inherited DNA sequence, which was fixed at conception, long before any adult disease.
This directional certainty is exactly why genetic variants are useful for causal inference (Mendelian randomization, Lecture 6). But finding a variant associated with a phenotype is still only an association: confounding, chance and linkage can all produce a spurious-looking association, so causality still has to be investigated.

section: 4.4 The additive model: β, SE and p
text:
4.4 The additive model: β, SE and p
The additive model (used for both phenotype types): compare the phenotype across the 0/1/2 groups, with each extra copy one unit of genotype dosage (the X variable).










Continuous (linear)
Binary (logistic)




β
Mean phenotype difference per extra allele (e.g. +0.2 mmol/L LDL-C, −1.9 mmHg)
Log-odds per allele; OR = exp(β) (β = −0.16 → OR = 0.85)


SE
Precision of β; depends on sample size, allele frequency and phenotype variability
Same dependencies


p-value
Evidence against \(H_0: \beta = 0\)
Evidence against \(H_0: \beta = 0\), i.e. OR = 1.00




“Worth noting” 1: genetic effects are small. The spread of phenotype values within each dosage group (from all the non-genetic factors) is usually much larger than the difference between group means. With a large enough sample you still detect the signal. GWAS is not about finding “the one cause”; hits are clues pointing to proteins involved in physiology or disease.





Simulated LDL-C by genotype dosage with a true effect of +0.2 mmol/L per allele. The group means (red) differ, but the spread within each group is far larger.




“Worth noting” 2: additive, dominant and recessive describe the genotype–phenotype relationship, not the allele. The same allele can act dominant for one phenotype and recessive for another. Most GWAS use additive models because they test many SNPs at once and the additive model is the simplest, most tractable default that works reasonably across all of them. Dominant/recessive models are more useful when studying one specific SNP or gene in depth.

title: Lecture 4 — From SNP to GWAS
text:
4.5 Covariates
\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 G + \beta_2 X_1 + \dots + \beta_n X_{n-1} + \varepsilon\]
\(G\) is genotype dosage; the \(X\)s are covariates such as age, sex, BMI and genetic principal components (PC1, PC2, …).
Why covariates are needed

Population structure. Allele frequency can differ between subpopulations, and the phenotype can also differ between them. Without adjustment you get a spurious SNP–phenotype association driven by structure, not biology (Section 4.9). The genetic principal components capture this.
Age, sex (and BMI). Often strong direct determinants of the phenotype. Adjusting removes their influence and reduces residual noise/confounding.
Technical variables. Genotyping batch, study center, or the batch/method used to measure the phenotype.







Warningβ is conditional on the covariates



The same SNP can have a somewhat different β in two studies that adjusted for different covariates. When comparing effect estimates across papers, check what was adjusted for.

4.6 The GWAS scan and summary statistics
GWAS = repeat the single-SNP regression separately for about 1,000,000 SNPs, one model per SNP, each adjusted, giving β, SE and p for every SNP. Conceptually simple but computationally heavy. Software: PLINK and regenie.
Practical notes: HG18 and HG19 are older reference genome versions (compare GRCh37/GRCh38 in Lecture 3). rsIDs refer to fixed variants but are not in genomic-position order, so sorting by rsID does not give positional order.
