title: Lecture 4 — From SNP to GWAS
section: 4.7 Multiple testing, Manhattan and QQ plots
text:
4.7 Multiple testing, Manhattan and QQ plots
Testing ~1,000,000 SNPs at \(p < 0.05\) would give about \(1{,}000{,}000 \times 0.05 = 50{,}000\) false positives by chance. The field’s standard threshold is:
\[p < 5 \times 10^{-8} \approx \frac{0.05}{1{,}000{,}000}\]
a Bonferroni-style correction for ~1 million independent tests (Bonferroni is formalized in Lecture 7). Significance at this level means a SNP is statistically robust, not that it is biologically important or has a large effect.
Manhattan plot. x-axis: genomic position ordered by chromosome; y-axis: \(-\log_{10}(p)\), so stronger associations are taller (“skyscrapers”). Each dot is one SNP. Horizontal lines usually mark a suggestive threshold (~5×10⁻⁵ or similar) and genome-wide significance (5×10⁻⁸).





Simulated Manhattan plot. Three loci contain a true signal; LD makes each one a tower of neighbouring SNPs rather than a single point.










WarningTwo interpretive caveats (stated explicitly in the slides)




A Manhattan plot shows where the strongest associations are. It does not tell you which variant or gene is causal.
A low p-value does not mean a large effect. With a huge sample, even a tiny effect reaches genome-wide significance.



QQ plot. Observed p-values plotted against those expected under the null (no association anywhere). Points bending away from the diagonal more than chance predicts can signal a systematic problem (uncontrolled population structure, technical/batch artifacts). But it can also mean the trait is highly polygenic: very many small effects spread across the genome. That is the lecture’s explanation for LDL-C’s QQ plot looking “a bit off”: benign and expected for a polygenic trait.





Left: null SNPs follow the diagonal. Right: a polygenic trait (many small true effects) lifts the whole upper tail. Uncontrolled population structure can produce a similar lift, so the plot alone does not tell you which.





  The SNP must have a large effect on the phenotype
  The SNP is the causal variant at this locus
  The association is statistically robust, nothing more
  The SNP explains a large share of phenotype variance
  A tiny p-value in a huge sample only says the association is unlikely to be chance. Effect size, causality and variance explained are separate questions (see rs11591147 in Section 4.10).

title: Lecture 4 — From SNP to GWAS
section: 4.8 Why one signal gives a cluster: lead SNP and r²
text:
4.8 Why one signal gives a cluster: lead SNP and r²
Nearby SNPs are correlated (in LD) because they are inherited together. So one true causal variant appears as many associated SNPs: every SNP in LD with it shows an association, not because it is independently causal but because it is correlated. If two SNPs are in LD, knowing one tells you about the other. The result is one peak in the Manhattan plot.
From the cluster you pick a representative, the lead SNP: usually the one with the smallest p-value. The lead SNP is not guaranteed to be the causal variant; it may just be a good proxy.
Quantifying LD: \(r^2\), the squared correlation between two SNPs’ genotypes (0 to 1).



\(r^2\)
LD strength




> 0.8
Very strong LD; close proxy


> 0.5
Moderate to strong


< 0.1
Weak


≈ 0
Essentially independent



Downstream analyses usually need independent variables, which raises the questions of how to find independent signals and the causal variant in a correlated cluster (Lecture 5), and the complication that the causal variant might not even be measured on the array.

4.9 Population structure and confounding
The problem. If ancestry-related differences in allele frequency coincide with differences in the phenotype across subpopulations (different countries, or distinct communities such as the Amish), a SNP can look associated with the phenotype even with no biological effect at all.










Frequency of allele G
Mean LDL-C




Population A
Higher

Population B
Lower
Lower


Pooled analysis
G looks associated with higher LDL-C, purely through the confounding, whatever G’s real effect





Standard mitigation strategies (likely asked as “how do you address population stratification in a GWAS?”):

Restrict the analysis to genetically homogeneous ancestry groups.
Adjust for genetic principal components (PC1, PC2, …).
Account for relatedness with mixed models (e.g. regenie).
Check the QQ plot and genomic inflation as a diagnostic.


  Adjusting for genetic principal components
  Restricting to one homogeneous ancestry group
  Using mixed models that account for relatedness
  Lowering the significance threshold to p < 0.05
  Stratification is confounding; a different p-value threshold does not remove it. The standard tools are homogeneous samples, PC adjustment, mixed models (e.g. regenie) and QQ/inflation checks.

\(0.015^2 = 0.000225\) (0.023%)




Lesson: a variant can have a large per-allele effect yet explain very little population-level variance because it is rare. Effect size and population relevance are different things; consider both.
Quantitative trait locus (QTL): a genomic region where genetic variation is associated with variation in a quantitative trait. More broadly, QTL analysis asks whether a variant can be linked to any measurable molecular trait: gene expression, protein level, metabolite level.
Protein QTL (pQTL): is the SNP near the gene encoding the protein (cis-pQTL) or elsewhere in the genome (trans-pQTL)? Developed in Lecture 8 (Section 8.9).






ImportantGWAS gives associations, not yet causality



GWAS gives you: a variant–phenotype association, an effect size, a p-value and a locus.
GWAS does not tell you: which SNP in the locus is causal, which gene is causal, which pathway is involved, or whether changing the molecular trait would change disease risk.
GWAS is a discovery tool. Causal inference needs extra assumptions and methods: Mendelian randomization (Lecture 6).

title: Lecture 6 — From GWAS to Mendelian Randomization
text:
Observational studies keep finding that people with high LDL cholesterol get more heart disease, but that alone cannot prove LDL causes it: smokers might have both, or early disease might change LDL. The gold standard answer is a randomized trial. Mendelian randomization (MR) uses a trial that nature already ran: at conception, each person is randomly dealt alleles that raise or lower LDL a little.
If people who inherited LDL-raising alleles also have more heart disease, and those alleles do nothing else relevant, the most plausible explanation is that LDL itself causes heart disease. Genotype cannot be changed by the disease, so reverse causation is ruled out from the start.
The whole method stands or falls on three assumptions about the genetic instrument: it must affect the exposure (relevance), it must not share causes with the outcome (independence), and it must affect the outcome only through the exposure (exclusion restriction). Most of the lecture is about checking those assumptions, especially the last one, which horizontal pleiotropy breaks.
This page covers imputation and proxy SNPs, the Bradford Hill criteria, why genes are good instruments, confounding, the three assumptions with their named threats, vertical vs horizontal pleiotropy, the Wald ratio and IVW estimate, weighted median and MR-Egger, and how to interpret an MR result. This is the lecture that ties the course together.

title: Lecture 6 — From GWAS to Mendelian Randomization
text:
6.1 Imputation and proxy SNPs
The problem. You want to know whether a specific variant (rsXY) affects a phenotype, but it was not measured in your data. Or: your data has SNPs + SBP, another dataset tested the same region against stroke, but the SNP overlap is poor: your lead SNPs are missing in the other dataset and vice versa. Dead end?
Two tools solve it, both using LD structure:







Tool
How it works




Proxy SNP
A SNP in very strong LD (\(r^2\) close to 1) with the SNP you want. It carries essentially the same signal, so it can stand in for it


Imputation
Uses LD patterns plus a large external reference panel to predict the genotype at a missing SNP as a (linear) combination of the measured SNPs, e.g. \(\text{SNP}_3 = \sum_{i \in \{3,5,6,8,11\}} a_i \cdot \text{SNP}_i\) (illustrative)



Both bridge the gap between studies (or a study and a reference panel) that did not measure exactly the same SNPs.

Criterion
Short meaning

2

5

title: Lecture 6 — From GWAS to Mendelian Randomization
text:
6.3 Genetic variants as instruments
Key insight: genetic variants are natural instrumental variables. Genotype is fixed at conception, so it comes first in any causal chain: no reverse causation (adult disease cannot change the genotype you were born with).
Genetic variant (SNP) ──▶ Exposure ──▶ Outcome
To use a SNP to study the causal effect of an exposure on an outcome, three core assumptions must hold: relevance, independence, exclusion restriction (Section 6.5 gives them in full).

title: Lecture 6 — From GWAS to Mendelian Randomization
text:
6.4 Why we need MR: confounding
Motivating problem. Does LDL-C cause coronary heart disease (CHD)? Observationally, high LDL-C precedes CHD, but how do you rule out:

confounding, e.g. smoking affects both: LDL-C ← SMOKING → CHD
selection bias
measurement error
reverse causation (which came first?)

The classical gold standard is the randomized controlled trial (RCT): intervene on LDL-C and see whether CHD risk changes. RCTs are expensive, slow, and not always ethical or feasible.
The genetic parallel. A naturally occurring SNP that raises or lowers LDL-C is allocated at random at conception, because meiosis randomly allocates alleles to offspring, much as an RCT randomly allocates treatment. Hence Mendelian randomization: SNP → LDL-C → CHD.










RCT
Mendelian randomization




Random allocation
Treatment assigned by researcher
Alleles assigned at meiosis


“Intervention”
Drug lowers LDL-C
Allele lowers LDL-C (lifelong)


Confounding
Balanced by randomization
Balanced, if the independence assumption holds


Reverse causation
Excluded by design
Excluded: genotype fixed at conception




Why is a GWAS association with CHD not enough? It says a SNP is associated with CHD (or LDL-C), not which pathway or which gene. The SNP could act through LDL-C, or through inflammation or blood pressure (SBP). MR is designed to resolve this.

section: 6.5 Instruments and the three MR assumptions
text:
6.5 Instruments and the three MR assumptions
Selecting instruments. Choose SNPs strongly associated with the exposure (e.g. LDL-C), typically \(P < 5 \times 10^{-8}\) in the exposure GWAS, and independent of each other (low LD, e.g. \(r^2 < 0.01\), via LD clumping, Lecture 5). At this stage you do not look at the SNP → outcome relationship at all; that comes in later.






ImportantThe three MR assumptions (the most important definitional block in the course)












#
Assumption
Meaning
Named threats




1
Relevance
The variant has a robust, strong association with the exposure. Usually checked by genome-wide significance in the exposure GWAS
Weak instruments bias and destabilize the estimate


2
Independence
The variant is not associated with confounders of the exposure–outcome relationship
Population stratification, assortative mating (non-random mate choice related to the trait), selection effects (participation depends on genotype and outcome)


3
Exclusion restriction
The variant affects the outcome only through the exposure
Horizontal pleiotropy: another pathway. Ask: “does this SNP affect the outcome through another pathway entirely?”

text:
6.6 Multiple instruments, dose–response and pleiotropy
With several independent instruments, each shifting the exposure by a different amount, plot each SNP’s effect on the exposure (β-exposure, e.g. β-LDL-C) against its effect on the outcome (β-outcome, e.g. β-CHD). Example SNPs: SNP1 (LDLR), SNP2 (LDLR), SNP3 (PCSK9), SNP4 (APOE), SNP5 (APOB), all genes with known roles in LDL metabolism. A consistent dose–response line (larger effect on exposure → proportionally larger effect on outcome) strengthens confidence in causality.
Pleiotropy: one variant affecting more than one trait or pathway.










Vertical pleiotropy
Horizontal pleiotropy




Path
SNP affects the outcome via the exposure
SNP affects the outcome through a pathway independent of the exposure


Example
SNP1 → PCSK9 → LDLR availability → LDL-C → atherosclerosis → CHD; or SNP2 → APOE → binding → same pathway
SNP3 → LDL-C → atherosclerosis → CHD, and SNP3 → inflammation → CHD


For MR
Not a problem: this is the causal chain MR is looking for
Bad: violates the exclusion restriction

title: Lecture 6 — From GWAS to Mendelian Randomization
text:
6.7 The Wald ratio and IVW
One instrument: the Wald ratio
\[\hat\beta_{MR} = \frac{\beta_{\text{SNP}\to\text{outcome}}}{\beta_{\text{SNP}\to\text{exposure}}}\]
“Change in outcome per genetically predicted unit change in exposure.” If the outcome is binary, β-outcome must be on the log-odds scale. The three assumptions must still hold.
Many instruments. Compute a Wald ratio per instrument (after LD clumping), then combine. If instruments give noticeably different ratios, that disagreement is informative: horizontal pleiotropy in some instruments, or weak instruments.
Inverse-variance-weighted (IVW) MR, the standard way to combine: a linear regression of β-outcome on β-exposure across the instruments, through the origin, weighted by precision. Equivalent to a weighted average of the Wald ratios:
\[\hat\beta_{IVW} = \frac{\sum_j \beta_{X_j}\beta_{Y_j}\,/\,\sigma_{Y_j}^2}{\sum_j \beta_{X_j}^2\,/\,\sigma_{Y_j}^2}\]
where \(\beta_{X_j}\) is SNP \(j\)’s effect on the exposure, \(\beta_{Y_j}\) on the outcome, and \(\sigma_{Y_j}\) the SE of \(\beta_{Y_j}\). (The slides describe the weights as the precision of the estimates, “or a combined variance term”; the formula above is the standard first-order version.)
Outlier instruments, whose Wald ratio deviates from the rest, can arise from:

pleiotropy / a different biological pathway
measurement error
a weak instrument
population differences between the exposure and outcome studies
chance

Agreement strengthens confidence; strong disagreement motivates sensitivity analyses.

6.9 Interpreting an MR result
An MR estimate is the expected change in outcome per genetically predicted change in exposure. Always check:

The unit of exposure: per 1 SD? per 1 mmol/L? a transformed scale? Without it the magnitude is meaningless.
Direction: \(\beta > 0\) → higher exposure increases outcome risk; \(\beta < 0\) → higher exposure decreases it.

For a binary outcome, report \(e^{\beta}\) as an OR per unit of exposure.

title: Lecture 8 — Proteomics
text:
DNA is fixed for life, but proteins change with diet, disease, drugs and age, and they are what actually does the work in cells. Most drugs act on proteins. That makes the proteome, all the proteins in a sample, an attractive layer for finding biomarkers and drug targets.
Measuring proteins is harder than reading DNA. Plasma contains proteins at concentrations that differ by many orders of magnitude, the same gene can give several protein forms, and most methods measure how much protein there is, not how well it works. Modern platforms (Olink, SomaScan) now measure thousands of proteins in tens of thousands of people, which allows proteome-wide association studies (PWAS), the protein version of a GWAS.
The second half connects proteins back to genetics. A SNP that changes a protein’s level is a pQTL. If it sits next to the protein’s own gene (cis-pQTL), it is a good instrument for protein Mendelian randomization: does genetically higher protein cause disease? The lecture closes the course’s PCSK9 story end to end.
This page covers why and where to measure proteins, the three technology families, what the numbers mean (NPX), QC and batch effects, PWAS, pQTLs (cis vs trans), protein MR and its specific pitfalls, colocalization and the path from association to mechanism.

title: Lecture 8 — Proteomics
text:
8.1 Why study the proteome?
Contrast from the molecular-layer table (Lecture 1): DNA is fixed, while RNA and proteins are dynamic, affected by diet, disease, drugs, environment and age. Proteins matter because they carry out cellular functions, act as signalling molecules, respond to disease/environment/diet/drugs/age, and are the targets of most drugs (Leqvio and Repatha in Lecture 3).
Worked example: insulin biosynthesis. “One gene” does not always mean “one direct protein”:
INS gene ─transcription─▶ INS mRNA ─translation─▶ preproinsulin
   ─signal peptide removed─▶ proinsulin
   ─folds, forms disulfide bonds, C-peptide cleaved out─▶ insulin + C-peptide
(Insulin is a signalling molecule central to metabolism, obesity and diabetes; compare the glucose/insulin example in Lecture 1.)
Proteins are not 1-to-1 with genes. Processes that multiply protein products:







Process
Example




Alternative splicing
One gene’s transcript spliced into several mRNA/protein variants


Cleavage
Insulin from proinsulin


Post-translational modification (PTM)
Phosphorylation, glycosylation, cleavage


Different cellular localization
Same sequence behaves differently depending on where it ends up


Protein complexes
Proteins assemble into larger units (quaternary structure, Lecture 1)



Net effect: the proteome is more dynamic and complex than the genome.






ImportantProtein amount ≠ protein function



More protein does not automatically mean more function (though in the simplest case it does). The same amount can have different function, e.g. after a GoF or LoF mutation (the PCSK9 examples in Lecture 3): a functionally altered protein can be present at a normal concentration. Most proteomics methods measure amount (abundance), not function.



  Every gene is translated into exactly one protein product
  Splicing, cleavage and modifications create extra variants
  Proteins are copied directly from other proteins in the cell
  The genome changes continuously with diet and age
  Alternative splicing, cleavage, post-translational modifications, localization and complex formation all multiply the number of distinct protein products per gene.

text:
8.2 Where can proteins be measured?







Sample type
Trade-off




Plasma / serum
Easily accessible; systemic, whole-body signal


Tissue
Needs a biopsy, but closer to the site of biology


Cells
Cell-type-specific mechanisms


Urine
Reflects kidney/urinary tract function and filtering


CSF (cerebrospinal fluid)
Relevant for neurological disease, but hard to obtain


Saliva, etc.
Accessible but more local; generally lower complexity/information than blood

text:
8.4 Three technology families











1. Antibody-based
2. Mass spectrometry
3. High-throughput affinity




Examples
ELISA, clinical immunoassays, Western blot
LC-MS
Olink, SomaScan


How
An antibody binds its target protein, giving a signal proportional to the amount
Protein digested into peptides with trypsin (cuts at lysine and arginine) → separated by liquid chromatography (LC) → charged by electrospray ionization → masses measured (“mass spectrum 1” = intact precursor peptide masses)
Each protein binds a specific engineered affinity reagent; the signal estimates relative abundance


Scope
Highly targeted: one or a few proteins
Can do discovery (unknown proteins/changes)
Thousands of proteins per sample


Quantification
Quantitative with calibration standards
Often calibrated with labelled control peptides
Relative abundance, not absolute


Strengths
Basis of routine clinical chemistry
Detects isoforms; discovery
Designed for large cohorts, biomarker discovery, PWAS


Weaknesses
Few proteins at a time
Technically complex; dynamic range needs dilution/preparation
Relative values only; assay binding can be affected by variants (8.11)




Real-world example: UK Biobank (UKBB) proteomics: about 50,000 individuals, about 3,000 proteins each.

  ELISA, since it is quantitative with calibration standards
  Mass spectrometry, since it can detect isoforms and discover
  Olink, since it measures thousands of proteins at once
  Western blot, since it uses a specific antibody per protein
  Antibody and affinity methods measure predefined targets. Mass spectrometry measures peptides directly, can separate isoforms and supports discovery.

section: 8.5 What a protein measurement means: units and NPX
text:
8.5 What a protein measurement means: units and NPX








Kind
Meaning
Units




Absolute concentration
Real physical amount
mg/dL (US), mmol/L (EU), ng/mL or pg/mL for low-abundance proteins


Relative abundance
Relationships between samples are meaningful, the numbers are not physical concentrations
Often normalized, log-transformed, arbitrary units



Platform units

Olink and SomaScan: relative abundance as NPX (Normalized Protein eXpression) on a log₂ scale. One NPX unit = a doubling of signal (same logic as log₂FC in Lecture 7).
Mass spectrometry: peptide intensity, ion counts or peak area; often calibrated by spiking in a labelled peptide of known concentration as an internal standard.


  The first person has 3 times as much
  The first person has 8 times as much
  The first person has 3 mg/dL more
  They differ by 3% in concentration
  NPX is log₂: a difference of 3 NPX means 2³ = 8 times the relative abundance. It says nothing about absolute mg/dL.

title: Lecture 8 — Proteomics
section: 8.6 QC, pre-analytical variation and batch effects
text:
8.6 QC, pre-analytical variation and batch effects
Pipeline: individual → blood sample → plasma/serum → assay → [QC, batch-effect handling, sample-prep issues such as freeze/thaw] → protein table (one row per person, one column per protein, e.g. Protein 1 … Protein 3000). Same shape as the GWAS table in Lecture 5, with continuous protein values instead of dosages.
QC at two levels







Sample-level QC
Protein-level QC




Was the sample measured successfully?
Is the protein reliably detected across samples?


Is it an outlier across many proteins (a sample-wide problem)?
Too much missingness for this protein?


Too much missingness for this sample?
Is the assay reproducible?


Did internal technical controls fail?
Is its variation dominated by batch rather than biology?



A very high or low value can be: real biology, contamination, technical failure, assay saturation (signal maxed out) or a processing error. Technical controls (for sample processing, hybridization/amplification, assay performance, normalization) help separate biology from artifact.
Pre-analytical variation (before the lab assay, often overlooked): fasting vs non-fasting, time of day, posture and recent exercise, tube/anticoagulant, time from draw to centrifugation, storage temperature, number of freeze–thaw cycles, hemolysis (red cells rupturing into the plasma), delay before freezing.






WarningSystematic, not random



Sick patients may be handled differently (more time, more controlled) than controls (processed faster, more randomly). Centers may have different protocols, and protocols change over time. If handling correlates with disease status, you get systematic bias.


Batch effects. A batch is any group of samples processed together that may share an artifact: the same plate, reagent lot, lab run, day, instrument or operator.
Detection: boxplots by plate/run (systematic shifts), PCA (do samples cluster by batch rather than biology?), clustering, technical controls, replicate samples across batches, comparing value distributions across plates.








Prevent: design stage
Correct: analysis stage




Randomize samples across plates
Normalize across platforms/batches


Balance cases and controls across plates/batches
Adjust for plate/run as a covariate


Technical replicate samples across plates
Include batch as a covariate in the regression (like genotyping batch in GWAS, Lecture 4)


Common reference samples repeated across plates





Transformations for proteomics data (right-skewed, wide dynamic range, sensitive to extremes):

log transformation compresses the right tail;
z-scores \(z = \dfrac{x - \text{mean}(x)}{\text{SD}(x)}\) (mean 0, SD 1) make effect sizes comparable across proteins on different scales;
plate normalization;
reference-sample normalization: the same sample on every plate, and all values on a plate normalized to it, removing plate-to-plate drift.


  The study cannot use NPX units for relative abundance
  Batch is completely confounded with case status
  Too few proteins are measured on each individual plate
  The protein values will no longer be right-skewed
  Any plate effect is indistinguishable from the case–control difference. Randomizing and balancing cases and controls across plates at the design stage prevents this; no analysis step can fully fix it afterwards.

title: Lecture 8 — Proteomics
text:
8.7 The proteome-wide association study (PWAS)
Same structure as a GWAS, with a protein instead of a SNP as the predictor:
\[Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{protein} + \beta_2 \times \text{age} + \beta_3 \times \text{sex} + \dots\]
If the protein is standardized (z-score), \(\beta\) is the effect of a 1-SD higher protein level:

continuous \(Y\): \(\beta = 0.18\) → 0.18 units higher outcome per SD;
binary \(Y\) (logistic): \(e^{0.18} \approx 1.20\) → 20% higher odds per SD.

Two model directions







Protein as predictor
Protein as outcome




\(Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{protein} + \text{covariates}\)
\(\text{protein} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{exposure} + \text{covariates}\)


Does this protein predict the phenotype?
Does this exposure predict the protein level?



Multiple testing in PWAS. ~3,000 proteins → about \(3{,}000 \times 0.05 = 150\) false positives at uncorrected \(p < 0.05\). In discovery, control the FDR (usually BH, Lecture 7). Unlike GWAS, there is no single conventional threshold like 5×10⁻⁸: it depends on the number of proteins, their correlation and the strategy.

title: Lecture 8 — Proteomics
text:
8.8 Association is still not causation
Three explanations for a protein–disease association:
protein ──▶ disease            causal
disease ──▶ protein            reverse causation (disease changes the protein)
protein ◀── confounder ──▶ disease   confounding
A protein can be a good biomarker/predictor without being causal. Troponin marks cardiac injury, but lowering troponin would not treat an MI: it is a readout of injury that already happened. Prediction and causation are different properties; only some proteins have both.

  Troponin cannot be measured in plasma with current assays
  It is released by injury, a consequence of the infarction
  Troponin levels are fixed at conception like DNA
  It is a trans-pQTL, so it has horizontal pleiotropy
  Troponin is a readout of cardiomyocyte damage. Lowering it would not undo the damage: prediction without causation.

title: Lecture 8 — Proteomics
text:
8.9 pQTLs: connecting genetics and proteomics
For a given SNP, do genotype groups (AA = 0, AG = 1, GG = 2) differ in protein abundance?
\[\text{Protein} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{Genotype} + \varepsilon\]
(The SNP → continuous phenotype model of Lecture 4 with protein level as the outcome.) Questions it answers: which variants regulate which circulating proteins? Which genes influence protein levels? Can a protein be linked genetically to disease? Can the variant be an MR instrument?
pQTL (protein quantitative trait locus): a SNP associated with a protein’s abundance.






WarningA SNP can change function without changing abundance



Since assays measure amount, a functionally important variant can be invisible to a pQTL analysis if it does not also change the concentration.


PCSK9 chain: PCSK9 SNP → circulating PCSK9 protein → LDL receptor activity → LDL-C. DNA to clinical biomarker in four steps.










cis-pQTL
trans-pQTL




Location
Close to the gene encoding the protein
Far away: common working definition > 500 kb, or a different chromosome


Plausible mechanisms
Transcription, splicing, protein stability or secretion of that gene’s product
Indirect: transcription factors, receptors, signalling pathways, protein-processing machinery


Interpretation
Relatively direct biological interpretation
More indirect


As MR instrument
Preferred
Higher risk of horizontal pleiotropy





  A cis-pQTL, because it changes protein abundance
  A trans-pQTL, because it is far from the encoding gene
  A cis-pQTL, because any SNP near a gene counts as cis
  Not a pQTL, because pQTLs must be on the same gene
  cis = near the encoding gene; trans = far away (> 500 kb) or on another chromosome. Different chromosome → trans.

title: Lecture 8 — Proteomics
text:
8.10 Protein Mendelian randomization
Genetic variant → protein abundance → disease risk. With \(\beta_{GP}\) = SNP effect on Protein and \(\beta_{GO}\) = SNP effect on Outcome:
\[\hat\beta_{MR} = \frac{\beta_{GO}}{\beta_{GP}}\]
The Wald ratio of Lecture 6 with protein level as the exposure: the effect on the outcome per genetically predicted unit change in protein.
Why cis-pQTLs are preferred as instruments: closer to the encoding gene, so an easier and more direct biological link, and less risk of horizontal pleiotropy (fewer alternative pathways than a variant acting at a distance). But cis-pQTLs still need all three MR assumptions (relevance, independence, exclusion restriction). Being cis reduces one risk; it does not remove the need for the other checks.

  0.05 log-odds per SD of protein X
  0.20 log-odds per SD of protein X
  5.0 log-odds per SD of protein X
  0.60 log-odds per SD of protein X
  β_MR = β_GO / β_GP = 0.10 / 0.5 = 0.20 per SD, i.e. OR ≈ e^0.2 ≈ 1.22 per SD higher genetically predicted protein X.

title: Lecture 8 — Proteomics
text:
8.11 Challenges specific to protein MR







Challenge
Why it matters




Horizontal pleiotropy
Violates the exclusion restriction; especially relevant for trans-pQTLs


Assay binding artifacts
A coding variant can change the protein’s structure so the antibody/aptamer binds worse, giving a seemingly lower level with no real change in amount. Fairly unique to protein instruments


Amount ≠ function
A variant can change activity, binding, stability or localization without changing measured abundance


LD can fake causality
SNP A affects the protein, a different SNP B in LD affects disease through another mechanism: protein and disease look linked only through the LD


One pQTL, many proteins
SNP → protein A, B and C at once; the effect may not run through the one protein you study



Colocalization: is it the same signal? Compare the pattern of association across a region for the protein’s pQTL and for the disease GWAS. If one shared causal variant drives both, SNPs in LD should give a matching pattern of association strength for both traits. If the patterns do not line up, the protein and disease associations are probably driven by two distinct (possibly nearby) causal variants. Check this before concluding that a pQTL and a GWAS hit at “the same locus” reflect the same biology.

  The variant may change assay binding, not the amount
  The variant must be a trans-pQTL since it is missense
  The variant cannot affect protein function at all
  The variant proves the protein causes the disease
  Coding variants can alter the epitope the antibody or aptamer binds, producing an apparent drop in abundance: an assay binding artifact.

Does changing its level or activity change cell function? Does it reproduce in an experimental model? Can the pathway be modified by a drug (is it druggable)?

title: Lecture 8 — Proteomics
section: 8.13 Reading material: eight plasma proteomics platforms on the same samples
text:
8.13 Reading material: eight plasma proteomics platforms on the same samples
(reading) Kirsher et al. (2025), “Current landscape of plasma proteomics from technical innovations to biological insights and biomarker discovery”, Communications Chemistry 8:279. This is the course’s reading material for Lecture 8. It puts numbers on the slides’ warnings: platforms measure different things, technical noise differs a lot, and “the same protein” on two platforms is often not the same measurement.
Design. Plasma from 78 healthy people (40 aged 55–65, 38 aged 18–22, half women) was measured on eight platforms: five affinity-based (SomaScan 7K and 11K with aptamers; Olink Explore 3072 and Explore HT with paired antibodies; NULISA, a small high-sensitivity antibody panel) and three mass spectrometry (MS) workflows (two discovery workflows that enrich low-abundance proteins with nanoparticles or remove high-abundance ones, and one targeted MS with internal standards, used as the reference because it gives absolute amounts).

Main results (numbers from the paper)







What was compared
Finding




Coverage
13,011 proteins in total; SomaScan 11K found the most (9,645). Only 36 proteins were measured by all eight platforms, 259 by all except NULISA


Technical CV (same sample measured repeatedly)
SomaScan about 5–6%, NULISA 6.6%, targeted MS 8.3%, Olink 3K 11.4%; Olink 5K 26.8% and the discovery MS workflows 26–30%


Data completeness (share of values above the detection limit)
SomaScan about 96%, Olink 3K 60%, Olink 5K 36%


Agreement between platforms (Spearman correlation for the same protein)
Two versions of one platform: about 0.75–0.8. Across technologies: often much lower, and bimodal: one group of proteins that agrees and one that does not


Age markers
Effect estimates of significant age proteins agreed well across platforms (correlation 0.66–0.95), much better than for all shared proteins (0.34–0.75)




Four lessons that link to the rest of the course

Technical vs biological variation (Lecture 7, 7.4). The paper compares the technical CV (replicates of the same sample) with the total CV across people. Where technical variation is a large share of the total, real biological differences are hard to see. Filtering Olink 5K to values above the detection limit lowered its CV from 26.8% to 12.4%, but removed about 40% of the analytes: precision is bought with coverage.
Missing values and noise go together. Proteins with many values below the detection limit, usually low-abundance proteins, also had the highest CVs. Plasma spans about 10 orders of magnitude in concentration, which is why low-abundance proteins are hardest.
Same name, different measurement. Affinity assays measure a binding epitope, not “the protein”. Most platforms measure total ApoE, but SomaScan’s “ApoE4” assay also binds ApoE2 and ApoE3 with similar affinity, so it is not isoform-specific; MS peptides unique to ApoE4 confirmed that NULISA’s ApoE4 assay is. This is the assay-binding issue of 8.11 in practice, and one reason why two platforms disagree.
Multiple testing changes the hit list. Each protein was regressed on age, sex, BMI and other factors, with significance by raw p < 0.05 and by Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted p < 0.05 (Lecture 7, 7.13). How many markers survived BH depended on each platform’s p-value distribution, not only on how many proteins it measured.

Pre-analytical factors. The introduction lists what can shift plasma protein levels apart from the biology of interest: age, sex, BMI and fasting status, and technical factors such as storage time, temperature, time of day, anticoagulant and processing protocol. Nanoparticle enrichment added platelet contamination. This is 8.6’s QC and pre-analytical variation with concrete examples.
Take-home. No platform is best at everything: affinity platforms give the broadest coverage and best precision, targeted MS gives absolute quantification, discovery MS can see proteoforms. Choose by study goal, and treat a protein measured on one platform as that platform’s measurement, not as a universal value.






NoteRead critically: a detail in Table 1





The footnote of Table 1 says that the Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used for categorical variables and the chi-squared test for continuous variables. That is reversed: Wilcoxon is a test for continuous (or ordinal) variables, chi-squared for categorical ones. Probably a typo, but the kind of thing worth noticing when reading a paper.




  The remaining proteins correlated worse with targeted MS
  About 40% of the analytes dropped out of the comparison
  Differences between people could no longer be estimated
  Low-abundance proteins had to be remeasured on SomaScan
  CV fell from 26.8% to 12.4%, but only because the noisy, mostly low-abundance analytes were removed: precision was bought with coverage.


  Because one platform reports NPX and the other log₂ units
  Because each binds its own epitope and may see other forms
  Because plasma proteins change too fast to measure twice
  Because correlation needs absolute, not relative, amounts
  Affinity assays measure whatever their binder recognises. Different epitopes, isoform selectivity (the ApoE example) and binding artifacts make two assays for one protein into two different measurements.

title: Seminar questions
text:
The seminar discusses computer exercises 1 and 2: GWAS on a synthetic phenotype, LD clumping, summary statistics from two GWAS, palindromic SNPs and two-sample MR. The focus is expected to be less on code and more on the concepts: why the numbers came out as they did and what you would do differently. Seminar content can also come on the written exam, so each question here is a module you can mark as reviewed.
Each module gives the lecturer’s question, then a model answer at the level of concepts. Questions that ask for your own numbers (“how many SNPs did you find?”) are answered with the reasoning only: fill in your own results from the exercises. The site is public, so it contains no results from the course data and no code for the exercises.

title: Seminar questions
section: S.1 Two causal variants, but more significant SNPs
text:
S.1 Two causal variants, but more significant SNPs






ImportantThe lecturer’s question



In exercise 1 you worked with a synthetic phenotype, generated from 2 variants. How many variants did you find before LD clumping? After clumping? Discuss how this could happen: how come more than two SNPs were significant before clumping, and how come more than two were left after clumping?


Your numbers: fill in from exercise 1.






TipModel answer





More than two significant before clumping. A causal variant’s signal is carried by every SNP in LD with it. If the causal variant changes the phenotype, any SNP whose alleles are correlated with it (r² well above 0) also shows a difference in mean phenotype, and with enough people that difference passes 5 × 10⁻⁸. Each causal variant therefore produces a tower of significant SNPs, not one SNP. A causal variant that was not itself genotyped is seen only through its tags.
More than two left after clumping. Clumping keeps SNPs that are not correlated with an already-kept SNP above the r² threshold within the window. Extra SNPs can survive when:

a SNP is in moderate LD with a causal variant (enough to be significant, below the r² threshold to the index SNP), so it survives as a “separate” signal although it tags the same variant;
SNPs tag the causal variant in different ways: two SNPs can each be correlated with the causal variant but only weakly with each other;
the SNPs lie outside the clumping window, so they are never compared with the index SNP, even if long-range LD links them;
the LD estimates come from a sample that differs from the GWAS sample (other ancestry, small reference), so r² is misestimated;
with a strong signal and a large sample, the tail of weakly correlated SNPs still reaches significance;
chance: a false positive passing 5 × 10⁻⁸ is rare but possible.

The general lesson: independent signals ≠ causal variants. Clumping gives a set of low-correlated SNPs, not the true causal variants, and the result depends on the r² threshold, the window and the LD reference. (If the two causal variants were themselves in LD, clumping could also give fewer than two.)
→ K.8 LD · → K.10 Clumping · → 5.3 Why neighbouring SNPs show up together




  Because clumping keeps every SNP below p = 5 × 10⁻⁸
  Because tags in weak LD with the index SNP are not removed
  Because clumping only removes SNPs on other chromosomes
  Because the additive model creates extra causal variants
  Clumping only removes SNPs whose r² with the index SNP is above the threshold inside the window. A tag of the same causal variant with lower r² to the index SNP survives as an apparently independent signal.

title: Seminar questions
section: S.2 Testing an exposure SNP in the outcome GWAS
text:
S.2 Testing an exposure SNP in the outcome GWAS






ImportantThe lecturer’s question



From the exposure GWAS you found a set of SNPs, and after LD clumping two SNPs remain: purple and black. The figure shows two overlapping sets: variants only in the exposure GWAS, variants only in the outcome GWAS, and variants in both. The purple SNP lies in the overlap; the black SNP lies in the exposure-only part. Explain how you would test whether the purple SNP also has an effect on the outcome, and how you could test the black SNP.








TipModel answer





Purple SNP (in both GWAS). Look it up directly in the outcome summary statistics. First harmonise: make sure β-exposure and β-outcome refer to the same effect allele (flip the sign of the outcome β if the alleles are swapped; check strand; handle palindromic SNPs, S.4). Then read the outcome β, SE and p, and compute the Wald ratio β-outcome / β-exposure with its SE.
Black SNP (only in the exposure GWAS). It cannot be looked up, so:

Use a proxy SNP: find a SNP in strong LD with the black SNP (for example r² ≥ 0.8) that is present in the outcome GWAS. LD must come from a reference panel of matching ancestry (for example 1000 Genomes EUR), since summary statistics contain no genotypes. Align the proxy’s alleles to the black SNP’s alleles through the haplotype (which proxy allele travels with the black SNP’s effect allele).
Impute the black SNP in the outcome data, if you have individual-level data or summary-statistic imputation.
Drop the instrument if no good proxy exists, and report that.

A proxy estimate is only as good as the LD: with r² < 1 the proxy’s association is diluted, and the LD in the reference panel may differ from the outcome population.
→ 6.1 Imputation and proxy SNPs · → 9.4 Finding the same variants · → 9.5 Harmonisation




  Use the exposure β in place of the outcome β
  Pick the nearest SNP in base pairs, whatever its LD
  Use a proxy SNP in strong LD that is in both files
  Lower the significance threshold for the outcome GWAS
  A proxy with high r² in a matching reference panel carries nearly the same information. Physical closeness alone is not enough; LD is what matters.

title: Seminar questions
section: S.3 Drawing the SNPs in linkage with each instrument
text:
S.3 Drawing the SNPs in linkage with each instrument






ImportantThe lecturer’s question



In the same figure (variants only in the exposure GWAS, only in the outcome GWAS, in both), with the black SNP (only in the exposure GWAS), the purple SNP (in both) and an orange SNP (only in the outcome GWAS): how would you picture the SNPs that are in linkage with each of them?








TipModel answer





Draw each marked SNP as the centre of a cloud of SNPs in LD with it, with the strongest LD (highest r²) closest. The cloud is defined by the genome and the population, not by which file the SNPs happen to be in, so each cloud crosses the borders of the sets:

Purple (in both GWAS): its LD partners are spread over all three areas. You do not need them, since purple itself can be used.
Black (only in the exposure GWAS): the useful part of its cloud is the part that falls inside the overlap. Any SNP there with high r² to black is a candidate proxy. If the cloud does not reach the overlap, no proxy exists.
Orange (only in the outcome GWAS): the mirror image of black. Its cloud can reach into the overlap and the exposure-only area. If the orange SNP is in strong LD with black, it is effectively the same signal measured in the other study, and it (or a SNP in both) can serve as black’s proxy. If it is not in LD with black or purple, it says nothing about those instruments.

A good way to draw it: concentric rings around each SNP for r² > 0.8, r² > 0.5 and r² > 0.1, overlaid on the circles. The rings show that “in which file” and “in LD” are two different properties.
→ K.8 LD · → 4.8 Why one signal gives a cluster

title: Seminar questions
text:
S.4 Palindromic SNPs






ImportantThe lecturer’s question



SNPs with alleles A/T and C/G are called palindromic. Can you guess why? Can you find out why they could be problematic in a two-sample GWAS analysis? Suggest ways to overcome the problem.








TipModel answer





Why “palindromic”. The complement of A is T and of C is G. For an A/T SNP the other DNA strand reads T/A, which is the same pair of letters; read on either strand it looks the same, like a word that reads the same backwards. For a non-palindromic SNP such as A/G, the other strand reads T/C, so a strand difference is visible.
Why it is a problem. Two GWAS can report alleles on different strands (forward vs reverse, different arrays or builds). For A/G vs T/C you can detect and fix this. For A/T you cannot tell from the letters whether “A” in file 1 is the same allele as “A” in file 2 or its complement. If you guess wrong, the outcome β gets the wrong sign, and the Wald ratio and IVW estimate are biased, possibly toward zero or in the wrong direction.
Ways to handle it:

Use allele frequencies. If the effect allele frequency is clearly away from 0.5 (for example below 0.4 or above 0.6), compare the EAF in both files: similar → same allele; mirrored (f vs 1 − f) → flipped. Requires similar ancestry in both studies.
Exclude palindromic SNPs with frequency close to 0.5, where the frequency cannot tell the alleles apart.
Replace the SNP with a non-palindromic proxy in strong LD.
Check strand information in the files (many GWAS report everything on the forward strand of a stated build), and report how many SNPs were excluded and whether results change without them.

→ B2 Allele alignment · → 9.5 Harmonisation







  Keep it and assume both files use the same strand
  Flip the sign of the outcome β to be on the safe side
  Exclude it, since the strand cannot be resolved
  Keep it, since palindromic SNPs need no harmonising
  Near 0.5 the frequencies cannot tell “same allele” from “complement”. The safe choice is to exclude the SNP or use a non-palindromic proxy.

title: Seminar questions
section: S.5 The clumping window: narrower or wider
text:
S.5 The clumping window: narrower or wider






ImportantThe lecturer’s question



In PLINK we used a window of 1,000 kb around the lead SNP. What do you expect to happen if the window is narrower or wider, for computation time and for the number of SNPs in linkage?








TipModel answer





The window sets which SNP pairs are compared with the index SNP. Only SNPs inside it can be removed for being in LD.










Narrower window (e.g. 250 kb)
Wider window (e.g. 5,000 kb)




Computation time
Shorter: fewer pairs to compute r² for
Longer: many more pairs (grows with the number of SNPs in the window)


SNPs found in linkage with the index SNP
Fewer: SNPs in LD beyond the window are never checked
More, up to the limit of real LD; far beyond the LD range, extra SNPs have r² ≈ 0 and are not removed anyway


Independent signals left
More, some of which may be the same signal (long-range LD missed)
Fewer, closer to truly independent; a little risk of removing a real second signal only if it is in LD above the threshold




Because LD usually decays within a few hundred kb, widening the window beyond the LD range adds computation but changes the result little. The r² threshold has a larger effect on the number of SNPs kept than the window, once the window covers the LD range. Regions with long-range LD (for example the HLA region on chromosome 6) are where a narrow window fails most.
→ K.10 LD clumping · → 5.4b r² bands and LD clumping




  Longer run time and the same or fewer independent SNPs
  Shorter run time and more independent SNPs left
  More SNPs pass the genome-wide significance threshold
  The r² values between the SNP pairs become larger
  More pairs are compared, so it takes longer; SNPs in LD beyond 1,000 kb can now be removed, so the number left stays the same or drops. r² values and p-values do not change.

title: Seminar questions
section: S.6 Two-sample MR: matching the files and the reference cohort
text:
S.6 Two-sample MR: matching the files and the reference cohort






ImportantThe lecturer’s question



In the two-sample MR (exercise 2): how many SNPs did you start with, and how many did you end up with? The lecturer pre-processed the data: can you guess how the two files were matched? How would you draw the reference cohort’s coverage in the figure (variants only in the exposure GWAS, only in the outcome GWAS, in both)?


Your numbers: fill in from exercise 2, and note at which step SNPs were lost (significance, clumping, matching, harmonisation).






TipModel answer





Why the number drops. At each step SNPs fall out: not genome-wide significant for the exposure; removed by clumping; missing in the outcome GWAS; missing in the LD reference, so they cannot be clumped; incompatible or ambiguous alleles (palindromic near 0.5) removed during harmonisation.
How the files could be matched. Most likely on the rsID, which identifies the variant independently of genome build, or on chromosome + position after making sure both files use the same build (hg19/GRCh37 vs hg38/GRCh38, lifting over one of them if needed). Then: keep only SNPs present in both, check that the alleles are the same pair (possibly on the other strand), align the effect allele and flip β where needed, and remove duplicates and multiallelic variants.
The reference cohort in the figure. Draw it as a third circle overlapping the other two. A SNP can be used as a clumped instrument only if it is in the exposure GWAS, the outcome GWAS (or has a proxy there) and the reference panel (to compute LD). The usable instruments are the intersection of all three. A SNP in the exposure–outcome overlap but outside the reference cannot be clumped and is usually dropped. The reference circle should match the ancestry of the GWAS (European reference for European GWAS).
→ 9.2 The data you need · → B1 Why an external reference is needed · → K.11 Summary statistics




  Every SNP that is significant in the exposure GWAS
  SNPs present in both the exposure and the outcome GWAS
  SNPs present in both GWAS and in the reference panel
  SNPs present in the reference panel and the outcome GWAS
  You need the exposure β (exposure GWAS), the outcome β (outcome GWAS) and LD for clumping (reference). All three must contain the SNP or a proxy.

title: Seminar questions
section: S.7 The code: problems and a more efficient version
text:
S.7 The code: problems and a more efficient version






ImportantThe lecturer’s question



Which part of the code did you have the most problems with? How did you solve it? Could you together come up with a more efficient code?


This is a discussion question about your own code, so there is no model answer. Prepare by noting one problem you hit and how you solved it. Points that usually come up, as concepts:

Reading large files: the GWAS file is large (around 200 MB); read only the needed columns, and filter on p before doing anything else.
Loops vs whole-column operations: looping SNP by SNP over harmonisation or Wald ratios is slow and error-prone; the same operations work on whole columns at once after the two files are joined on SNP ID.
Letting PLINK do the heavy work: clumping and LD are faster with PLINK’s built-in functions than with your own pairwise r² code.
Checks at every step: count SNPs after each filter, and check allele alignment on a few SNPs by hand before trusting the totals.
Reproducibility: one script from raw files to result, with fixed thresholds stated at the top, so the numbers in S.1 and S.6 can be regenerated.

title: Seminar questions
section: S.8 GLGC vs 1000 Genomes: allele frequencies and reference allele
text:
S.8 GLGC vs 1000 Genomes: allele frequencies and reference allele






ImportantThe lecturer’s question



Discuss similarities and differences in the allele frequencies and the reference allele between GLGC (the Global Lipids Genetics Consortium summary statistics) and 1000 Genomes.








TipModel answer





What each dataset is. GLGC is a meta-analysis of GWAS of blood lipids: summary statistics per SNP from many cohorts, mostly of European ancestry. 1000 Genomes is a reference panel of individual genotypes from a few thousand people in 26 populations, used here for LD.
Similarities. For the same SNP (same rsID) in European-ancestry samples, allele frequencies are usually close, because both mainly describe European populations. Large disagreement is a warning sign.
Differences in allele frequency:

Ancestry mix: GLGC pools cohorts of different composition; 1000 Genomes EUR is about 500 people, all-population 1000 Genomes is much more diverse. The frequency in the full 1000 Genomes can differ a lot from GLGC.
Sample size and precision: a frequency from about 500 people is much noisier than one from a large meta-analysis.
Imputation and QC: GLGC frequencies may be averages over cohorts with different arrays and imputation quality.
Which allele the frequency refers to: GLGC gives the frequency of its A1 (effect) allele; 1000 Genomes files give the frequency of the ALT allele. The same SNP can show f in one and 1 − f in the other without any real difference.

Differences in the reference allele:

In 1000 Genomes (VCF/PLINK files) the REF allele is the base in the reference genome sequence at that position, and ALT is the other one. REF is not necessarily the major allele.
In GLGC, A1 is the effect allele chosen by the analysis, not tied to the reference genome. It is neither “the reference” nor necessarily the minor allele.
Genome build: GLGC files use older builds (hg18/hg19 positions), the 1000 Genomes data in the exercises use hg38, so positions differ while rsIDs stay the same.
Strand: alleles may be reported on different strands, which is invisible for palindromic SNPs (S.4).

Practical consequence: always align on the actual alleles, not on “A1” or “REF” labels, and use the allele frequencies as a check for flips and palindromic SNPs.
→ K.3 MAF · → 3.3c Genome builds · → B2 Allele alignment




  The minor allele in the European population
  The effect allele from the published GWAS
  The base found in the reference genome sequence
  The allele that raises the trait being studied
  REF is defined by the reference genome assembly. It can be the major or the minor allele, and it has nothing to do with which allele a GWAS reports effects for.
